The initiative aligns with Ontario’s Energy for Generations plan, which aims to meet a provincial electricity demand forecast to grow to 90% by 2050.

The Nanticoke Generating Station, which was North America’s largest coal-fired generating station, operated from 1972 to 2013. It was safely demolished in 2019. “OPG understands the critical importance of engaging with communities early when considering siting new generation infrastructure,” said OPG President & CEO Nicolle Butcher. “This funding will ensure Haldimand County has the capacity to engage fully on behalf of its residents as we work collaboratively to explore generation options for this site.”

In December 2024, Haldimand County passed a motion of support for OPG to explore potential energy redevelopment at Nanticoke. The site has a number of strategic advantages. It is approved for up to 3,000 MW of electricity generation and features extensive pre-existing transmission infrastructure as well as having access to rail lines, port facilities, and major highways. It is located within an established manufacturing region.

A nuclear facility at this location could run for 65 years. The multi-year plan would generate thousands of skilled trades positions. Public consultations, environmental evaluations, and regulatory approvals are still to be completed. However, the funding helps to establish a formal memorandum of understanding between OPG and Haldimand County.

“Ontario has a plan to breathe new life into OPG’s Nanticoke Generating Station site, after the former government shuttered this job creator,” said Stephen Lecce, Ontario Minister of Energy & Mines. “Our government has a vision to generate power and jobs across Haldimand County by planning for new energy generation that fully unlocks the region’s full potential. To meet electricity demand that is forecast to increase by as much as 90% by 2050, we are planning ahead and building for future generations. We are taking another step forward to advance this project, in true partnership, including seriously considering small modular reactor deployment, to revitalise the economy and workforce.”

This new funding, which will be used at the discretion of the municipality, will help Haldimand County further assess the site for future development, including evaluating municipal infrastructure improvements that would be required to support the siting of new generation. OPG has provided similar funding to local Indigenous Nations to support early engagement activities. OPG will continue to work with Indigenous Nations, municipal leadership, and local stakeholders to understand their priorities and determine support for various generation technologies.

OPG will also continue to work with both the local municipality and Indigenous Nations to discuss potential economic and social benefits that would flow to host communities, including equity participation options for Indigenous Nations, municipal funding to support infrastructure investments, and associated jobs and economic development opportunities for local community members.

The Nanticoke site already hosts a new 44 MWe solar plant – Nanticoke Solar – built in partnership with the Six Nations of the Grand River Development Corporation and the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation. The facility was put into service in March 2019, on schedule and on budget.

In addition to Nanticoke, OPG is exploring new generation opportunities at two other strategic sites – Wesleyville in Port Hope, where a new large-scale nuclear development is being proposed, and Lambton in St Clair Township.

In February 2026, OPG signed a partnership agreement with the Municipality of Port Hope to advance planning and preparation for the world’s largest nuclear generating station at the Wesleyville site. The project would support 10,500 jobs across Ontario, including 1,700 new good-paying jobs in Port Hope, representing an average 15-20% boost to overall employment levels in the local area, while contributing CAD235bn to Ontario’s GDP over its lifespan.

Like Nanticoke, Lambton is a former heavy coal-fired generation plant site. OPG is running impact assessments to preserve long-term options for the property. Ongoing talks with local municipal and Indigenous leaders determine which energy mix (nuclear, storage, or renewables) is most appropriate.

title: Serbia initiates Phase 1 nuclear plans
author: Tracey
text: The initiative will strengthen regulatory frameworks, develop nuclear expertise and prepare the country for potential deployment of 1,200 MW of nuclear capacity after 2040.Share
(Photo credit: Serbian Energy Ministry)

Serbia’s Minister of Mining & Energy Dubravka Đedović Handanović has signed a partnership agreement with Électricité de France (EDF) and the French Development Agency (AFD), which launches Phase 1 of Serbia’s civilian nuclear programme. AFD provided a €500,000 grant ($576,000) to support building professional and organisational capacities in Serbia aimed at improving the knowledge and experience of personnel involved in the nuclear programme.

Serbia’s nuclear programme has rapidly progressed from a 35-year moratorium on nuclear construction to an active institutional planning phase, operating in strict alignment with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)

. This framework mandates that any country introducing a civilian nuclear programme must evaluate and systematically build out 19 specific infrastructure issues across three progressive development phases. Serbia has now embarked on Phase 1.

In October 2024, the Ministry contracted EDF and French consultancy Egis to perform a Preliminary Technical Study on the Peaceful Use of Nuclear Energy. EDF delivered a 19-step framework in March 2025, in line with the IAEA
establishing critical milestones across three phases. It established that Serbia needs roughly €30m to fully navigate the pre-construction regulatory and administrative hurdles.

In November 2024, the National Assembly voted to lift the 1989 legislative ban that prohibited the construction of NPPs, processing facilities, or nuclear waste sites. The Serbian Energy Sector Development Strategy was formally amended to integrate 1,200 MWe of nuclear capacity into the grid in line with post-2040 decarbonisation goals.

The Nuclear Energy Programme Implementing Organisation (NEPIO) was set up in February 2026 and became fully operational in July. NEPIO is tasked to steer national policy, alongside SRBATOM, the Serbian Radiation and Nuclear Safety and Security Directorate (Direktorat za radijacionu i nuklearnu sigurnost i bezbednost Srbije).
In July, the Ministry held an extensive, four-day structural workshop alongside the IAEA to audit the legal, environmental, and supply-chain vulnerabilities of the grid. To complete Phase 1 of the
, Serbia has committed to completing 18 comprehensive studies. EDF will author three of these primary technical studies, while the remaining 14 are being opened to international tender.

“Our goal is that by the middle of next year, all studies will be completed that will enable an informed decision to be made on the further development of the nuclear programme, said Handanović. “In the years ahead, Serbia must be ready in the institutional, regulatory and professional sense for the choice of technology, and Serbia could get its first nuclear plant after 2040.”

She said: “EDF is the leading operator of nuclear power plants globally, with more than 50 nuclear reactors in France alone and is the world leader in the production of electricity from sources with low carbon dioxide emissions. It is very important for us that at this stage of our nuclear programme, in which we are laying the foundations for nuclear energy in our country, we will be able to use their knowledge, experience and resources, which will be of great use to the experts of the National Body for the Implementation of the Nuclear Energy Development Programme (NEPIO).”

She added that the most important part of this project relates to the development of a human resources. “Personnel represent the most valuable element in the development of the nuclear program in every country, and one of our most important tasks will be the creation of a base of engineers and other personnel who will be able to responsibly and professionally manage nuclear facilities in Serbia in the future,” she said.

AFD’s €500,000 grant represents its first participation in the field of nuclear programme development. With these funds, support will be provided in building professional and organisational capacities necessary for the preparation, development and management of Phase I and part of Phase II of the nuclear programme. The main activities include strengthening the competencies of institutions and professional teams, developing personnel capacities, developing project and management skills, improving safety culture, as well as acquiring technical knowledge necessary for making informed decisions, in accordance with the IAEA recommendations.

title: UPDATE: Europe’s heatwave strains nuclear output
author: Tracey
text: To date, six reactors across Europe are closed and another 17 are facing restrictions due to severe heatwaves and critically low river levels, as operators respond to environmental and cooling water constraints.Share
Critically low water levels on the Danube River in Romania (Credit: Reuters via Facebook)

At least 15 nuclear reactors have been temporarily shut down or had their power output curtailed across Europe due to severe heatwaves and critically low river levels during June and July. While no plants have been directly closed by wildfires, the Sizewell B nuclear power station in the UK has been placed on “high alert” due to a major 100-acre wildfire burning just four miles away.

The vast majority of disruptions have occurred in France, where state-owned EDF is legally bound to close reactors or reduce power to prevent discharged cooling water from pushing river temperatures past environmental thresholds. Switzerland’s Beznau NPP has also been impacted. A record-breaking drought has caused the Danube River to drop to historic lows affecting NPPs in Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria resulting in the imminent full closure of the Paks NPP in Hungary and the possible closure of Romania’s Cernavodă NPP.

As of 3 August, there are six nuclear units closed across Europe and 17 units facing restrictions. In France, unit 3 at the Bugey NPP on the Rhône River closed on 9 July and unit 2 at the Golfech NPP was fully shut down on 30 July as Garonne river temperatures surged. Units facing restriction on output include Bugey 4&5, Saint-Alban 1&2 (Rhône River), Blayais 1&3 (Gironde Estuary), Nogent-sur-Seine 1&2 (Seine River), Chooz 2 (Meuse River), and all four units at Tricastin (Canal de Donzère-Mondragon/Rhône).

Output at Switzerland’s Beznau NPP on the Aare River (units 1&2) is also curtailed. Both reactors were taken completely off the grid on 26 June when the Aare River first spiked to the 25°C threshold and remained offline for several weeks. They are currently capped at roughly 50% of normal generation capacity to limit environmental thermal pollution.

The situation for NPPs on the Danube River is critical. In Hungary, three of the four units are now offline with the fourth expected to close shortly. Unit 3 closed on 29 July, unit, unit 1 was closed on 1 August and unit 4 on 2 August with the closure of unit 2 imminent. on throttled, and the entire 2 GWe plant’s overall output has fluctuated to near 10% capacity with a complete shutdown imminent because the Danube has dropped below intake pump levels. The river has collapsed to less than one-third of its normal seasonal flow.
Hungary’s mitigation efforts focus heavily on emergency energy rationing, massive electricity imports, and alternative transport rules to protect the grid from the near-total loss of the Paks NPP.

All heavy rail cargo transport across Hungary is strictly banned between 5:00 PM and 10:00 PM. Budapest has turned off decorative and architectural lighting for major landmarks. Citizens are under strict instructions to voluntarily limit the use of high-draw appliances like air conditioning and washing machines during peak hours. Nearly 300 major corporations have voluntarily slashed production to avoid forced power cuts. The government has established a rolling grid-disconnection protocol for heavy manufacturing factories if voluntary caps fail to stabilise the network.

State grid operator Mavir previously used temporary legal waivers allowing Paks to discharge hotter wastewater into the Danube. However, with the river physically too shallow for the suction nozzles, this mitigation is no longer effective. To decouple the national grid from the Danube River, the government announced a plan to use private capital and EU funding to fast-track 4 GWe of wind energy capacity by 2030.

In Romania, unit 1 at the Cernavodă NPP was closed on 28 July and unit 2 is fluctuating under critical, hour-by-hour output restrictions. Unit 2 is operating at restricted, approximate half-capacity. If emergency measures fail, authorities warn the entire plant must be completely shut down by 6 August at the latest.

The Romanian naval forces have deployed explosives in the Danube River near Izvoarele. By blasting apart massive rock formations and sandbars, they are successfully forcing a larger volume of water to divert toward the Cernavodă nuclear plant to keep its remaining active reactor cool. Romania is also building temporary dams and barriers in the riverbed to artificially raise water depth right at the plant’s suction nozzles. Romania’s government has declared a nationwide state of alert in the energy sector and is appealing to citizens to voluntarily limit electricity usage during peak evening hours.

Bulgaria is also on the verge of a severe grid emergency, with the government warning that it may be forced to initiate a complete shutdown of its entire nuclear sector within days. Bulgarian Energy Minister Iva Petrova warned on 29 July 2026 that the country may be forced to temporarily shut down both of its operational units – units 5&6 at the Kozloduy NPP.

To prevent Kozloduy’s cooling systems from failing, the Bulgarian Energy Minister established direct contact with the Serbian Ministry of Mining and Energy. They are actively coordinating with the Djerdap 1 (Iron Gates) hydropower complex located upstream. Serbia is strategically releasing water through its dam system to help maintain the Danube’s level just above the critical operating thresholds required by Kozloduy.

Bulgaria has classified the current crisis as a force majeure event, noting that the river is continuing to drop by up to 2 centimetres every day. In response, the Kozloduy plant has deployed emergency “special measures”, including riverbed dredging and the preparation of secondary pumps to try and keep the intake channels clear enough to avert an immediate blackout.

The energy minister established direct contact with the Serbian Ministry of Mining & Energy. They are coordinating with the Djerdap 1 (Iron Gates) hydropower complex located upstream. Serbia is strategically releasing water through its dam system to help maintain the Danube’s level just above the critical operating thresholds required by Kozloduy.

Unfortunately, significant river and hydrological relief is not expected anytime soon, with meteorologists and grid experts projecting that low river levels will continue to threaten European nuclear plant operations until at least mid-August. Longer-term weather models suggest that substantial rainfall may not arrive until late autumn.

title: ZNPP faces fresh security threats
author: Tracey
text: The IAEA has warned that rising military activity, drone incidents, power disruptions and damage to critical infrastructure are heightening nuclear safety and security risks at Ukraine’s Zaporizhia nuclear power plant.Share
(Image credit: ZNPP on Telegram)

Increased military activity near the Zaporizhia NPP (ZNPP) and the city of Energodar, where many plant staff live, further challenges efforts to maintain nuclear safety and security at the site, Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said in his latest update on 30 July.

He referred to a two-day internet outage from midday on 27 July the longest such disruption since the IAEA established its continued presence at the site almost four years ago. It was not immediately clear what caused the internet loss. ZNPP also continued to face water supply difficulties, although groundwater wells continue to provide water for essential safety and security functions at the plant. Military activity near the ZNPP and Energodar remains a serious concern, he said. “The recent internet outage and water supply problems are further examples of the challenges facing those who operate the plant under already difficult and stressful circumstances.”
The plant subsequently faced drone attacks. ZNPP reported on its

channel on 30 July that an unmanned aerial vehicle with a live charge was recorded on the territory of the ZNPP in the area of the site of the used fuel dry storage facility. “The drone was found in the immediate vicinity of the storage building of a conveyor designed to transport containers with used nuclear fuel. The ammunition was defused in a timely manner. There were no casualties or damage,” ZNPP said.

It added: “However, the attack itself is an extremely dangerous incident. The conveyor is a unique specialised equipment that has no analogues. Its damage could deprive ZNPP of the ability to safely perform routine transportation and technological operations with used nuclear fuel. This would mean a disruption of the plant’s technological capabilities for handling used nuclear fuel, significantly complicating the necessary routine operations and creating additional risks for the long-term safe operation of the facility.”

The same day, ZNPP experienced an hour-long technical outage of external power supply during which the station’s systems were powered by backup diesel generators. ZNPP said the radiation background remained within normal limits and the station’s needs were met through the back-up 330 kV Ferrosplavnaya-1 power line. The 750 kV high-voltage Dneprovskaya power transmission line remains unconnected, although repairs have been completed. However, Ukraine still has not yet supplied voltage to the line.
The following day, a drone struck the gallery connecting all six units at the ZNPP,

reported, citing Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev. He said that the station’s personnel were moving along the gallery at the time. The impact occurred a few metres away from the reactor compartment of unit 3. ZNPP Communications Director Yevgeniya Yashina confirmed the attack and said IAEA staff had been informed.

An unmanned aerial vehicle was discovered in the immediate vicinity of the unit 3 building, near the wall of the transition gallery, which is used by the station’s operational personnel on a daily basis. There was no detonation. There were no damages or injuries, according to the station. Reporting the incident on its

channel, ZNPP said: “This is the second time in the last week that a drone has been found on the territory of the ZNPP. For the second time in a week, the target of the attack is facilities directly related to ensuring the safe operation of the NPP.”

ZNPP added: “Such actions pose additional risks to nuclear safety and once again demonstrate that the attacks are no longer limited to the perimeter of the plant, but are taking place in close proximity to critical facilities. Despite the ongoing provocations, ZNPP staff continue to monitor all safety parameters. The plant is in a safe state, and the radiation levels on the site and in the monitoring area do not exceed natural levels.”

title: Hanford tank waste reclassified as LLW
author: Tracey
text: Managing the treated liquid as low-level radioactive waste will enable waste from Hanford’s S, SX and U Tank Farms to be processed faster and provide expanded disposal options.Share
Layout of tank farms at the Hanford site in Washington (Credit: US DOE)

The US Department of Energy (DOE) has finalised a Waste Incidental to Reprocessing (WIR) determination to reclassify specific treated tank wastes from the S, SX, and U Tank Farms in the 200 West Area at the Hanford site in Washington. This decision allows DOE to legally manage and dispose of this material as low-level radioactive waste (LLW) rather than high-level waste (HLW).

The finalisation of this evaluation carries several critical implications for the broader clean-up mission at the Hanford Site. Shifting the waste management classification allows for expedited retrieval and processing. The reclassification supports the implementation of alternative immobilisation methods, such as grouting, as outlined under regional environmental agreements. Managing the treated liquid as LLW opens up possibilities for commercial disposal at specialised facilities outside Washington state. By diverting large volumes of low-activity waste from the Hanford Vitrification Plant, the site can reserve vitrification capacity for the highest-radioactivity streams. However, the waste must still undergo strict processing to remove key radionuclides to the maximum extent technically and economically practical.

The determination follows completion of DOE’s technical evaluation, an independent review by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and consideration of public comments. It concludes that the waste, following separation, pretreatment and solidification, is not high-level radioactive waste and meets DOE criteria for management as LLW.

The proposed disposal strategy for the grouted waste from Hanford’s S, SX, and U Tank Farms strictly avoids local disposal. Instead, under the West Area Risk Management (WARM) Project and the 2025 Holistic Settlement Agreement, the DOE is executing a “glass-plus-grout” dual strategy. This mandates shipping the stabilised low-level waste entirely outside of Washington State.

The waste will be permanently stored at one of two primary commercial disposal facilities. EnergySolutions (Clive, Utah) operates a massive commercial facility in the West Desert of Utah, roughly 75 miles west of Salt Lake City. This specialises in the near-surface disposal of Class A LLW. Waste Control Specialists (WCS) in western Texas operates a highly engineered, near-surface disposal facility built over dense red-bed clay formations. It is licensed to accept Federal Waste Streams, including Class A, B, and C LLW.

Before reaching these final burial grounds, the liquid tank waste will undergo pretreatment at Hanford. Radionuclides (such as caesium-137) are separated from the liquid matrix on-site using ion-exchange technology. The pretreated low-activity liquid is transferred off-site to a local commercial contractor – primarily Perma-Fix Northwest in Richland, Washington – where it is mixed with a cementitious matrix to form solid, stable grout blocks. Once solidified and safely encased, the final grouted waste containers are transported to either Utah or Texas using specialised trucks or railcars.

The underground storage tanks at the Hanford Site constitute the largest accumulation of highly radioactive nuclear waste in the Western Hemisphere. They were built during World War II and the Cold War to support the US nuclear weapons arsenal and now present one of the most complex environmental clean-up challenges in history.

Between 1944 and 1989, Hanford’s nine nuclear reactors synthesised 74 tonnes of plutonium, roughly two-thirds of the total US stockpile. Five large onsite processing facilities (canyons) dissolved used uranium fuel to extract plutonium. This chemical extraction process left behind 56m gallons of highly toxic, chemically complex, radioactive liquid byproducts.

The waste is distributed across 177 underground storage tanks buried under 10 feet of soil and gravel to shield workers from radiation. The tanks are organised into 18 distinct groups called tank farms. The architecture is divided into two eras. The 149 Single-Shell Tanks (SSTs) were constructed between 1943 and 1964 out of a single carbon-steel inner liner surrounded by a thick, reinforced concrete shell. They hold between 55,000 and 1m gallons each. They are long past their intended 20-year design life and 67 are known or suspected to have leaked over 1m gallons of waste into the surrounding soil and groundwater.

The 28 Double-Shell Tanks (DSTs) were constructed between 1968 and 1986 and feature an extra “tank-within-a-tank” steel barrier with a monitored space (annulus) to detect internal leaks before waste escapes into the environment.

The tanks are organised into 18 distinct groups – tank farms – divided geographically between two primary operating zones known as 200 East Area and 200 West Area. The 88 tanks in the 200 West Area are all SSTs. This area includes the S, SX, and U farms involved in the low-level waste reclassification. The U tank farm hold 16 SSTs built 1943–1944); the S tank farm holds 12 SSTs built 1950–1951; and the SX tank farm hold four SSTs built 1953–1954.

The contents of the tanks are not uniform fluids. Over decades of chemical shifts, evaporation, and settling, the inventory has separated into three distinct layers, roughly split into equal thirds. A dense, heavy layer at the bottom of the tanks has a consistency resembling wet beach sand. It contains most of the high-level radionuclides (strontium and plutonium). Above that is a hard, crusty, concrete-like layer formed when liquid waste evaporated, locking up highly water-soluble salts. Then there is the highly alkaline, intensely radioactive liquid layer hovering above or trapped within the saltcake and sludge matrix.

To mitigate the risk of further catastrophic leaks, crews utilize specialised robotic arms and high-pressure liquid sluicing to scrape, scour, and pump out the remaining solids from the ageing single-shell structures. As of mid-2026, DOE has successfully emptied waste from 23 of the 149 SSTs, moving the retrieved material into newer double-shell tanks to await final stabilisation via glass vitrification or out-of-state grouting.

title: Russia’s nuclear icebreaker fleet advances
author: Tracey
text: The Project 22220 vessel is scheduled for delivery in 2028 and will support year-round Arctic navigation along the Northern Sea Route.Share
The RITM-200 reactor is a modern nuclear power plant designed for Russian icebreakers and potential terrestrial use (Credit: Atommedia)
The second RITM-200 reactor for Russia’s

icebreaker has been completed at Rosatom’s ZiO-Podolsk plant near Moscow Rosatom noted that the construction of any nuclear icebreaker is an extraordinary event in itself. “But the construction of Leningrad is of particular importance. It was no coincidence that the icebreaker received its name in honour of the hero city. In 2024, when the whole country celebrated the 80th anniversary of the lifting of the siege of Leningrad, veterans and blockade survivors took the initiative to name the newest nuclear icebreaker after the Northern capital. And the President of the Russian Federation supported this.”
Rosatom continued: “Last year we resumed the tradition of assigning proper names to special reactor plants. The reactor installations of the future nuclear icebreaker
were named Ilya and Dobrynya – in honour of the Russian heroes. This year, after consulting with veterans and blockade survivors, we jointly decided to assign the names Iskra and Grom to the
reactors – in honour of the military operations, thanks to which it was possible in 1943-1944 to first break through the blockade ring, and then completely liberate besieged Leningrad.”

Symbolism often goes hand in hand with advanced technology, Rosatom said. “In the next 40 years, our RITM-200 reactor plants will perform the strategic task of breaking through multi-metre ice as part of the most powerful icebreaker in the world, ensuring uninterrupted navigation of ships along the Northern Sea Route and forming a reliable transport frame for the most important logistics artery of our country.”

Rosatom’s mechanical engineers gave unofficial comical names to the first RITMs. These were names that reflected how the reactor plants behaved during assembly – Affectionate, Grumpy and others. In 2025, the new RITM-400 reactor plants for
were given official names for the first time – Ilya Muromets and Dobrynya Nikitich.

Currently, 13 small reactor plants for nuclear icebreakers and small NPPs are at various stages of production. This is a record for Russia’s nuclear industry. Several enterprises of Rosatom’s Mechanical Engineering Division are involved. In St Petersburg the metallurgical blanks are produced for the future reactor plants. In Nizhny Novgorod the internal devices for RITMs are being developed. The designer, overall supplier and manufacturer of internal devices for the RITM-200 and RITM-400 reactor units is OKBM Afrikantov. The production of the reactor vessels and control assemblies are carried out at ZiO-Podolsk.
In addition to the icebreaker fleet, reactor units of the
will be used in small nuclear energy projects Rosatom is constructing in Yakutia and Uzbekistan, and in floating power units developed to supply power to remote areas with access to sea.

icebreaker is being built at the Baltic Shipyard (Baltiysky Zavod) in St Petersburg. It is the sixth vessel belonging to the Project 22220 design series, representing the largest and most powerful nuclear icebreakers in the world. The ship’s keel was laid down in January 2024. As of mid-2026, construction is roughly 31% complete, moving slightly ahead of its initial schedule. The ship is planned to be commissioned and delivered to the Arctic fleet by December 2028. RITM reactors are already operating on new generation icebreakers (project 22220)
. Three more nuclear-powered ships of the same project are under construction –
In 2018, the Russian Government vested Rosatom with the powers of an infrastructure operator for the Northern Sea Route (NSR). The corporation oversees the federal project
Development of the Northern Sea Route
, and is involved in implementing the development plan for the NSR to 2035 as well as the initiative for the socio-economic development of the Russian Federation to 2030,
Year-round Northern Sea Route

. One of Rosatom’s strategic goals is to make the NSR an effective transport artery connecting Europe, Russia and the Asia-Pacific region. In December 2024, a federal project for development of the Great Northern Sea Route – a transport corridor from St Petersburg and Kaliningrad to Vladivostok – was approved.

title: BEST tokamak moves toward 2030 goal
author: Tracey
text: The BEST tokamak bridges the gap between China’s EAST research device and the planned CFEDR, providing a key testing platform for future fusion power.Share
The Burning Plasma Experimental Superconducting Tokamak (BEST) facility, currently under construction in Hefei, Anhui Province, China (Credit: Atomic Energy 2.0)

Construction of China’s Burning Plasma Experimental Superconducting Tokamak (BEST) is being carried out at an accelerated pace. BEST, located in the Sanshigang parish of Liuyang district of Hefei in Anhui province, acts as an intermediate testing phase between China’s record-breaking Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST) and the planned Chinese Fusion Engineering Demo Reactor (CFEDR).

Unlike EAST, which focuses on sustaining high temperatures, BEST is specifically engineered to achieve and study a self-sustaining “burning” deuterium-tritium plasma. The reactor aims to demonstrate net fusion energy production, targeting an unprecedented five-fold energy gain (Q=5). BEST is built to demonstrate fusion-based pilot power generation, moving beyond purely academic plasma research. The goal is to demonstrate net energy gain from fusion and produce the world’s first fusion-generated electricity around 2030.

Recent aerial footage shows the massive circular construction site where the device is taking shape, complete with heavy machinery and dozens of workers assembling its multi-layered structure deep in the ground. Located in the Future Great Science City in Hefei, the facility spans a campus of approximately 160,000 square metres. The main unit’s 400-tonne base was installed in late 2025. It serves as a massive vacuum insulation container designed to withstand a total equipment load of over 6,000 tonnes. Scientists from more than 10 countries, including France, the UK, and Germany, have already signed the Hefei Fusion Declaration to collaborate on the project.

In July 2026, two of the reactor’s superconducting magnets passed full-load testing, a major milestone with the facility on track for completion by the end of 2027. With the successful completion of these tests, project officials confirmed that 100% of the core technologies have now been localised.

The Institute of Plasma Physics at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (ASIPP) completed the development, acceptance, and full-performance testing of the two superconducting magnet systems, namely a toroidal-field superconducting magnet and a high-temperature superconducting central solenoid coil.

The 582-tonne D-shaped toroidal field coil is 1.3 times the size of the TF magnet used in the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER), and its energy storage capacity is three times greater, according to its developers at ASIPP. The institute has been developing the magnet for six years.

In the future, 16 such magnets will be combined and built together to form a complete Toroidal Field. “Its function is to confine the plasma, preventing it from hitting the walls within the vacuum chamber,” said Wu Yu, a researcher at ASIPP. “The intensity of its magnetic field is related to the temperature and density required for the plasma in the future. A ring composed of 16 coils will generate a magnetic field of 6.5 teslas.”

Song Yuntao, head of the ASIPP noted: “This coil is the heaviest in the world, with the highest energy storage capacity among all superconducting coils currently. The special stainless steel we are currently using, as well as our insulating materials and superconducting materials, are all domestically produced. This project is realised with 100% of domestic products.”

The magnet was built and tested under a major national research programme called CRAFT (Comprehensive Research Accompanying Facility for Fusion Technology). CRAFT is an overarching test facility in Hefei built by the Institute of Plasma Physics. It develops and evaluates components for China’s next-generation reactors. While EAST served as the engineering foundation to develop this technology, its physical design is far too small for a 21-metre-tall, 582-tonne magnet component.

title: Korea, UAE eye Vietnam reactor bid
author: Tracey
text: Both countries aim to combine Korean reactor technology with Emirati financing as Vietnam expands its nuclear energy programme.Share
(Image credit: EXCEL Services Corp.)

South Korea’s TeamKorea, which includes Korea Electric Power Corporation (Kepco) and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) are looking to enter Vietnam’s nuclear power market in partnership with the United Arab Emirates (UAE). South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry & Energy in July held high-level talks in Hanoi with Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry & Trade, proposing a plan for Korea and the UAE to jointly construct the Ninh Thuan 2 nuclear power project.

Vietnam’s Ninh Thuan nuclear project plans a total of four reactors in the Ninh Thuan region. The Ninh Thuan 1 project is being constructed by Russia and the Ninh Thuan 2 project was originally to be constructed by Japan. However, when Japan gave up its preferred bidder status and decided to withdraw from the project, Korea saw an opportunity to enter Vietnam’s nuclear power market.

Korea is hoping to enhance its competitiveness in the global nuclear export market by combining its large-scale reactor construction capabilities with the UAE’s oil wealth. Should the Korea-UAE alliance win the Vietnam contract, it would provide a springboard for the revival of Korea’s nuclear export prospects. These have been seriously disadvantaged following a lengthy legal battle with US-based Westinghouse over intellectual property, which effectively resulted in Korea’s exclusion from the European market (except the Czech Republic).

The government’s proposal for a three-way Korea-UAE-Vietnam cooperation, acknowledges that the UAE’s abundant financial capacity could serve as leverage in winning the project. “In financing, the UAE has the capacity to offer bold and competitive interest rates,” a Korean official said. “If Korea’s technology combines with the UAE’s funding, it will not fall behind in competition with China and France.”

South Korea had earlier agreed with the UAE to expand strategic cooperation in the nuclear power and plant sectors, building on team Korea’s successful construction of the UAE’s Barakah NPP. During his visit to the UAE last November, Korean President Lee Jae-myung noted: “The success of the UAE’s Barakah nuclear plant opened a new chapter in energy cooperation between the two countries…. We will also pursue ways for the two countries to jointly enter the global nuclear power market.” Minister of Trade, Industry and Energy Kim Jung-kwan visited the UAE in June, meeting with high-level officials from key nuclear power institutions to discuss formation of a cooperation framework for jointly entering promising nuclear markets in third countries.

Meanwhile, US nuclear consultancy company EXCEL Services Corporation, has announced the formation of EXCEL Services Vietnam, a wholly owned subsidiary, with the aim of expanding its presence in Vietnam as the country advances plans to develop nuclear power as a critical source of reliable electricity to support continued economic growth.

“Vietnam has demonstrated a strong commitment to developing nuclear power as an important electricity generation source, and EXCEL is proud to support the country’s efforts to establish safe and effective nuclear power operations,” said EXCEL President & CEO Dr Donald Hoffman. “We look forward to being part of this important and exciting journey.”

EXCEL named James Voss as General Director of EXCEL Services Vietnam and has established offices in Hanoi City and Ho Chi Minh City. EXCEL has already entered into memoranda of understanding with the Vietnam National Innovation Centre (NIC) and the Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology. Additional cooperation agreements are under development with strategic government agencies and corporate partners.

Vietnam’s strategy for the peaceful development and deployment of nuclear energy to 2035, with a vision towards 2050, expects nuclear power to account for 6-8% of total electricity output. As well as the construction of four large-scale nuclear power units, the plan includes and 10-15 small modular reactors.

According to the revised Power Development Plan VIII, Vietnam aims to bring Ninh Thuan 1 and 2 into operation between 2030 and 2035, with a combined capacity of 4,000-6,400 MWe. By 2050, an additional 8,000 MWe of nuclear capacity will be required to provide stable baseload power, with the potential for further expansion depending on demand.

title: Japan sets reactor rebuild target
author: Tracey
text: The move aims to offset ageing reactor retirements and rising power demand from AI data centres, while preserving a path to roughly 20% nuclear generation by fiscal 2040.Share
(Image credit: Climate Scorecard)

Japan has decided to revise its nuclear energy policy guidelines to include a target of “rebuilding” 2-5 nuclear power reactors by the 2040s. In Japan’s nuclear energy guidelines, “rebuild” (often translated as “replace” or “reconstruct”) means constructing brand-new, next-generation reactors directly within the sites of existing, decommissioned power plants. Instead of building entirely new nuclear facilities in new locations, the government is initially replacing retired units with modern ones.

The decision was adopted at a meeting of relevant Cabinet ministers led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. “We will move forward with policies to ensure investment in nuclear power plants,” Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said at the meeting, suggesting that the government will also promote programs to nurture human resources.

The aim is to mitigate a projected power supply shortage in the 2040s due to the decommissioning of ageing reactors that have been in operation for 60 years and to address increased demand driven by the surge of AI data centres and advanced manufacturing.

The target for the 2050s is to expand the replacement initiative to build an additional nine reactors, bringing the cumulative total to 11 to 14 new reactors. The final 14-plant fleet is projected to supply 16 GWe of new capacity. The goal is to double nuclear power’s current share in the national grid, aiming for it to supply roughly 20% of Japan’s electricity by fiscal year 2040, up from roughly 8.5% in 2023. Reliance on coal, natural gas, and oil will be reduced from the current 60–70% down to 30–40%.

Anticipating possible opposition to the plan, Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa announced a revised framework to advance surveys for high-level radioactive waste final disposal sites while offering higher relief incentives to local municipalities. More than 40,000 public comments were submitted opposing the expansion, fuelled by persistent post-Fukushima trust issues and recent seismic safety scandals at other regional plants.

The plan could face other obstacles. A recent Nikkei Asia assessment revealed that 70% of companies in Japan’s nuclear sector face critical difficulties recruiting specialised staff and engineers. The 20% target requires bringing Japan’s broader idle fleet back online. Out of 33 operable units, only 15 have cleared post-Fukushima safety standards to resume operations.

The government is shifting funding through the New Energy & Industrial Technology Development Organisation (NEDO) to speed up the integration of small modular reactors (SMRs) and advanced safety designs. The revised guidelines preserve the safe decommissioning of Tokyo Electric Power Company’s (Tepco’s) Fukushima Daiichi NPP as the state’s highest structural priority.

The government has not yet published an official, definitive list identifying specific reactor sites for the 2040s rebuild strategy. However, according to the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) and industry utility opinion, specific locations have emerged as the clear priorities based on their operational history, recent restarts, and active site surveying.
The selection process for candidate sites automatically favours those that meet three criteria:
Sites housing reactors built in the 1970s and 1980s that will hit their strict 60-year operational limits by the 2040s;
Plants where utilities have already spent billions upgrading seawalls, backup generators, and seismic defences to pass NRA’s modern safety protocols; and
Areas where local governors and town councils are receptive to the newly revised, higher government relief incentives for hosting nuclear infrastructure and waste surveys.

Fukui Prefecture (the “Nuclear Coast”) is the frontrunner for early rebuilds due to its high concentration of existing reactors and relatively cooperative local municipalities. Kansai Electric Power Co’s Mihama NPP is currently the most prioritised site for the new rollout. Kansai has already revived and initiated targeted geological and topographical on-site surveys to prepare for the construction of a next-generation reactor. The utility is actively planning to deploy the SRZ-1200, an advanced 1,200 MWe light-water reactor developed by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries designed with enhanced safety features. Units 1 and 2 at Mihama have already been permanently shut down and are undergoing decommissioning, providing an ideal open footprint.

Kansai’s Takahama NPP, also in Fukui Prefecture, is also heavily prioritised for long-term planning because its units were among the first ageing reactors successfully restarted under the strict post-Fukushima safety standards. However, Takahama houses two units that are among the oldest in the country and will reach their maximum 60-year operational lifetimes before 2040.

Sendai NPP in Kagoshima Prefecture is also widely cited in government strategy drafts as a primary candidate. Kyushu Electric has announced formal considerations for next-generation innovative reactors to meet surging regional grid demands, heavily driven by new local AI data centres. The site has a pre-existing blueprint originally intended for a third unit (Sendai-3) that was abandoned after the 2011 Fukushima disaster, meaning substantial preliminary siting work is already complete.

In Hokkaido Prefecture, Hokkaido Electric Power Co’s Tomari is another candidate. Following the Nuclear Regulation Authority’s (NRA’s) safety approval of Tomari unit 3 in July 2025 (targeted for full commercial restart by 2027), this site has risen significantly in priority. As the youngest operable reactor site in the country, its existing grid connections and updated safety infrastructure make it highly viable for next-generation expansion.

In Niigata Prefecture, Tepco’s seven-unit Kashiwazaki-Kariwa NPP, as one of the largest nuclear plants in the world, is critically important to Japan’s grid. The commercial restart of unit 6 in April represents a regulatory milestone for Tepco. Because the infrastructure here is massive and capable of handling high-capacity outputs, it is technically an elite candidate for future co-located replacement reactors. However, unlike other Japanese utilities permitted to build new reactors, Tepco is currently restricted solely to restarting existing assets due to trust issues and financial burdens from the Fukushima cleanup.

title: Dutch SMR projects gain traction
author: Tracey
text: McDermott and ULC-Energy have agreed to support potential deployment of Rolls-Royce SMRs in the Netherlands, integrating nuclear power with industrial decarbonisation projects.Share
Rendering of a proposed Small Modular Reactor (SMR) power station designed by Rolls-Royce SMR (Credit: ULC-Energy)

US-based engineering and construction company McDermott and Netherlands nuclear development company ULC-Energy have signed a cooperation agreement to support deployment in the Netherlands of Rolls-Royce SMR projects. This includes the integration of small modular reactors (SMRs) with energy-intensive industrial processes.

The agreement is expected to leverage McDermott’s expertise in energy transition and industrial decarbonisation, including low-carbon hydrogen and ammonia, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and carbon capture and use (CCU), combined with ULC-Energy’s nuclear project development capabilities.

“This agreement builds on our existing relationship with ULC-Energy and reflects our shared commitment to advancing low-carbon energy solutions in the Netherlands,” said Rob Shaul, McDermott’s Senior Vice President of Low Carbon Solutions. “With a long-standing presence in the country and a major hub in The Hague supporting projects across Europe, we bring the engineering and execution expertise needed to support the development of Rolls-Royce SMR projects and their integration into industrial energy systems.”

Dirk Rabelink, CEO of ULC-Energy, noted: “At ULC-Energy, we see nuclear as most effective when integrated into energy systems. SMRs offer the flexibility to deliver electricity, heat or hydrogen where it creates the greatest value. Our previous collaboration with McDermott demonstrated the strength of this approach, and we look forward to further expanding our cooperation in other applications.”

The strategic partnership marks a major step forward for clean energy infrastructure in the Netherlands. By merging heavy engineering execution with nuclear project development, the agreement builds on a successful 2023 hydrogen cogeneration study to turn SMRs into multi-purpose industrial utilities.

The framework relies on the Rolls-Royce SMR design, a 470 MWe small pressurised water reactor built 90% in factory conditions to minimise on-site construction risk. The core focus is pairing SMR heat and power directly with energy-intensive sectors to manufacture low-carbon hydrogen, green ammonia, and SAF. SMR-generated electricity will power CCU networks to capture and re-purpose industrial emissions.

McDermott joins an established network of regional industrial partners compiled by ULC-Energy, including Siemens Energy, BAM, Mammoet, and Bureau Veritas, Urenco, Orano and Fugro, supporting the delivery of SMR-powered energy solutions in the Netherlands and Belgium.

McDermott and ULC-Energy previously collaborated in 2023 on a study assessing the industrial-scale production of hydrogen using a Rolls-Royce SMR power plant coupled with a Solid Oxide Electrolyser (SOEC). ULC-Energy was project coordinator and McDermott provided engineering design and cost input for the balance of plant and heat integration systems.

The deployment of Rolls-Royce SMR technology in the Netherlands is governed by a primary exclusive development agreement, which subsequently spawned a web of strategic engineering and regulatory partnerships. In August 2022, Rolls-Royce signed an exclusive deployment agreement designating ULC-Energy as its exclusive nuclear project developer in the Netherlands. This agreement established the 470 MWe factory-built pressurised water reactor as ULC-Energy’s choice technology for the region.

ULC-Energy and Rolls-Royce SMR have both signed secondary cooperation agreements to build a local supply chain, engineering framework, and regulatory path. In January a collaboration agreement was signed with France-based Bureau Veritas to oversee the industrial-scale safety, certification, and risk compliance of the reactors.

In 2025, structural agreements were signed to support turbine/generator supply chains and nuclear fuel cycle logistics Rolls-Royce SMR signed a global partnership agreement selecting Siemens Energy as its conventional island technology partner and the exclusive supplier of steam turbines, generators, and auxiliary systems for the SMR fleet. ULC-Energy signed a cooperation agreement France’s Orano establishing logistics frameworks for handling, transport, and temporary storage of used fuel tailored to the Dutch SMR infrastructure.

In November 2023 a memorandum of understanding (MOU) was signed between Rolls-Royce SMR and BAM Infra to explore infrastructure, civil engineering, and construction logistics within the Dutch landscape.

These private and corporate agreements run parallel to the Dutch government’s broader climate policy. The coalition government in December 2021 earmarked €5bn ($5.75bn) in cumulative nuclear funding to 2030 to build new standard reactors and establish the regulatory framework for SMR deployment. This initial €5bn baseline has since been expanded by subsequent governments. The 2024 and 2026 Outline Coalition Agreements added funding from the Climate Fund. This increased the target pool to €9.5bn to 2035 to expand the Netherlands plans for two large-scale reactors to a minimum of four plants, including SMRs.

title: China approves eight new reactors
author: Tracey
text: The projects will deploy Hualong One and Guohe One technologies as the country accelerates its nuclear expansion strategy.Share
(Photo credit: China Science via Facebook)

China’s State Council ​has approved the construction of four nuclear power projects comprising eight ​generating units. Total investment in ⁠the projects is estimated at ​more than CNY170bn ($25.2bn). The projects include two ​units each in Zhejiang, Guangdong, ​Liaoning and Shandong provinces.

The newly approved nuclear projects include two units each for phase II of Jinqimen NPP in East China’s Zhejiang Province, phase III of Taipingling NPP in South China’s Guangdong Province, Phase I of the Zhuanghe NPP in Northeast China’s Liaoning Province, and Laiyang NPP in East China’s Shandong Province.

Phase II of CNNC’s Jinqimen NPP will use China’s third-generation Hualong One Version 2.0 technology and will include private capital participation. Once fully completed, the six-unit site will support power supply and green transition in Zhejiang and the Yangtze River Delta.

The upgraded Hualong One Version 2.0 will also be deployed at the Taipingling plant, with each unit having a capacity of 1,217 MWe megawatt, CGN Power Co said. Once complete, the six-unit plant is expected to generate over 55 TWh annually. Phase I of CNNC’s new Zhuanghe NPP will use standard Hualong One technology.

The new Laiyang plant will construct two 1,543 MWe Guohe One units – China’s independent third-generation technology, SPIC Industry-Finance Holdings Co said. The project marks the start of large-scale, standardised construction of Guohe One units. Once complete, the six-unit Laiyang project, with total investment of CNY128.3bn, is set to become China’s biggest NPP by installed capacity.
China has approved 49 nuclear reactors since 2022, with a total investment of nearly CNY1,000bn signalling a new phase of rapid development for the Chinese nuclear power industry.

Hualong One is a third-generation, pressurised water developed by CNNC and CGN. Ten Hualong One units are in commercial operation, both domestically and internationally, with 37 more approved or already under construction.

Guohe One is a third-generation nuclear power technology developed by State Power Investment Corporation (SPIC), with fully autonomous intellectual property rights. The first Guohe One unit of the Rongcheng nuclear power project in Shandong has already entered commercial operation, while the second unit is in the commissioning phase.
In April, China’s total ⁠installed nuclear power capacity was put at 125 GWe, with ⁠60 nuclear units in commercial operation and 36 under construction.

title: ORNL launches fusion testbed partnership
author: Tracey
text: The FULCRA initiative will combine government research capabilities and private investment to validate critical reactor components.Share
The leadership team from ORNL and Rutherford Energy Ventures (Credit: ORNL)

The US Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and fusion energy consultancy Rutherford Energy Ventures (REV) have begun development of a new public-private partnership framework to create shared fusion testbed infrastructure at ORNL. The new consortium model, the Fusion Upscaled Leveraged Consortia for Rapid Acceleration (FULCRA), is designed to address gaps identified in the DOE Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap by providing a novel design and funding model for Fulcrum test facilities at national laboratories.

By pooling federal research assets with private investment, this model creates shared Fulcrum test facilities to help private commercial developers validate expensive reactor subsystems. The consortium focuses heavily on testing components that must survive extreme reactor environments. These include:
Plasma-facing materials: testing armour tiles that line inner reactor walls against temperatures reaching tens of millions of degrees Celsius.
Fuel breeding blankets: validating the modules responsible for absorbing heat and breeding tritium fuel.
Radiation-hardened materials: creating materials capable of withstanding intense, multi-decade neutron bombardment.
Sensors and controls: qualifying reactor-compatible electronics and control systems under extreme magnetic and thermal pressure.

The development is structured as an 18-month, two-phase programme anchored at ORNL. During the first nine months, experts from REV will review the lab’s facilities. They will examine ORNL’s work in fusion materials, blanket design, and high-energy neutron sources. They will also gather technical feedback from commercial fusion firms. The final nine months will focus on designing the first pilot testing facility. This includes creating the engineering blueprints and the financial structure. Once built, private developers will use the facility to test their prototypes and collect real performance data.

For an individual organisation, the cost would be high to build the integrated test facilities required to validate commercial designs and advance the readiness of critical fusion plant components. The consortium model pools federal capabilities with private sector investment to build specialised testbeds for validating critical fusion subsystems. This testbed infrastructure will translate decades of foundational research investment into world-class infrastructure that would be shared with the broader community.

The collaboration combines ORNL’s deep expertise in fusion science and technology, established partnership network and unique facilities with REV’s technical fusion knowledge and expertise in capital and ecosystem development.

Venture capital company REV was founded, specifically to spur the private funding of the fusion ecosystem, by two MIT professors – Dennis G Whyte (inventor of the world’s strongest high temperature superconducting magnets that are key to fusion technology) and Andrew Lo (designer of the financial model that launched the US biotech industry) –

“ORNL’s leadership in fusion science, materials and neutron science makes it well-suited to anchor this shared infrastructure. This collaboration gives us the opportunity to build a partnership model that can serve the entire fusion ecosystem and be replicated across the national laboratory system,” said Troy Carter, director of ORNL’s Fusion Energy Division.

REV Partner & Managing Director Guinevere Shaw said the fusion field has the science but lacks the testing infrastructure to translate that science into validated, commercial-ready technology. “No single entity can build that alone. FULCRA is designed to solve exactly that problem, anchored at ORNL where the scientific foundation already exists.”

Arnold Lumsdaine, public-private partnerships lead in ORNL’s Fusion Energy Division, noted: “ORNL has spent decades building its fusion programme and relationships across the public and private sectors. The lab is positioned to be a national leader to meet today’s challenges, not just as a research institution, but as a partner and collaborator towards commercialisation.”

Once the pilot facility is running, the team will publish its framework as a standard guide. Other national laboratories can then use the blueprint to build similar test sites. This network will establish clear safety standards for fusion hardware and help train the technical workforce needed for commercial power plants.

title: EDF taps Technip for EPR2 buildout
author: Tracey
text: The non-exclusive deal will place Technip’s project and construction specialists inside integrated teams with EDF as France pushes ahead with six new EPR2 reactors.Share
The Penly Nuclear Power Plant has been selected for two new EPR2 reactors (Credit: Technip Energies)

Technology and engineering company Technip Energies has signed a strategic framework agreement with EDF to accelerate the execution, construction management, and delivery of EDF’s EPR2 nuclear new-build programme. Under this non-exclusive agreement, Technip Energies will embed experienced project management and construction specialists directly into integrated teams alongside EDF personnel.

EDF will draw on the proven expertise of Technip Energies in the delivery of major complex industrial and energy projects to help strengthen execution discipline and improve schedule predictability across all EDF’s nuclear new-build activities.
announced in February 2022

, envisages the construction of six upgraded EPR reactors with an option for eight more. The first three pairs of EPR2 reactors are planned for the Penly, Gravelines and Bugey NPP sites. Construction of the first EPR2 reactor at Penly was then expected to start in 2027 with an estimated programme cost of €51.7bn ($59.5bn), which was revised to €67.4bn in 2023 and to €72.8bn in January. The target for commissioning the first reactor has since been revised to 2038 with the others to follow at intervals of 12-18 months.

The programme, which will be the subject of state support measures, was submitted for approval to the European Commission (EC) in November 2025 with a view to taking a final investment decision at the end of 2026. Regulators are concerned that subsidising the fleet will
entrench EDF’s dominant 75%+ market share

of French electricity production, preventing new commercial players from entering the market. The EC is specifically auditing three pillars of the €72.8bn programme – a subsidised state loan that covers 60% of construction costs; a 40-year contract for difference (CfD) price guarantee; and a formal risk-sharing mechanism that shields EDF from delays.

The EPR2 initiative was designed directly to address and fix the systemic project failures of the first EPR construction projects at Flamanville 3 in France and Olkiluoto 3 in Finland – both of which were delayed by around a decade and massively over budget. There were multiple causes for this. Construction of Flamanville 3 started in 2007 before completing technical engineering blueprints. Years were lost repairing heavy-section penetration and safety welds. France had not built a domestic commercial nuclear reactor since 1996 and EDF passed excessive risk to external suppliers, causing severe execution blockages.

The partnership between EDF and Technip Energies is a direct response to the project failures seen at Flamanville 3 and Olkiluoto 3. Bringing in Technip Energies injects proven, large-scale industrial project discipline to stabilise the EPR2 timeline and prevent a repetition of those delays. Technip’s primary mandate is to establish strict project execution discipline to guarantee schedule certainty. Technip brings decades of experience managing ultra-complex international energy infrastructure.

With the targeted commissioning date for the first EPR2 pair at Penly already pushed out from 2035 to 2038, the need for rigorous external project oversight is critical. Instead of acting as a hands-off external consultant, Technip is embedding its managers directly inside EDF teams to oversee construction sites and the supply chain.

“This agreement marks a new chapter between EDF and Technip Energies,” said Loïc Chapuis, President Project Delivery and Services at Technip Energies. “By combining EDF’s long-standing nuclear expertise with Technip Energies’ experience in delivering highly complex industrial and energy infrastructure, our integrated teams will support execution and schedule certainty across major nuclear projects. Beyond the operational benefits, this partnership reflects the kind of long-term industrial cooperation needed to deliver France’s nuclear ambitions and support the future of the EPR2 programme.”

Thierry Le Mouroux, Group Senior Executive Vice President with responsibility for the Nuclear Projects and Industrial Partnership Division at EDF, noted: “This strategic partnership combines the complementary expertise of both companies. The EDF Group brings its mastery of reactor engineering and an efficient supply chain dedicated to building EPR2s, while Technip Energies contributes its world-renowned complex project management skills. Together, we strengthen the French nuclear team to ensure the EPR2 program is delivered successfully—on time, within budget, and to the expected levels of safety.”

title: Fukushima begins latest wastewater discharge
author: Tracey
text: The IAEA says the tritium level in the latest batch is far below Japan’s operational limit and consistent with international safety standards.Share
Storage tanks containing treated radioactive wastewater at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant (Credit: Government of Japan)

Japan has begun another discharge to the sea of nuclear-contaminated wastewater from the crippled Fukushima Daiichi NPP – the 22nd such release since the operation began in 2023. Plant operator Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings (Tepco) said about 7,800 tonnes of wastewater containing approximately 1.3 trillion becquerels of radioactive tritium will be released into the ocean. The discharge – the fourth for fiscal 2026, is scheduled to continue until 17 August.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed that the tritium concentration in the Advanced Liquid Processing System (ALPS)-treated water is far below Japan’s operational limit and consistent with international safety standards.

The ALPS system removes 62 types of radionuclides, except for tritium (3H), a radioactive isotope of hydrogen. In addition, carbon-14 (C-14), potassium-40 (K-40), strontium-90 (Sr-90), iodine-129 (I- 129), and some isotopes of caesium (Cs) and plutonium (Pu) remain in the water, albeit in smaller quantities.
As part of its ongoing safety review, the IAEA independently
tested samples from the latest batch
before the release began. Analysis at the site showed that the tritium levels were far below Japan’s operational limit of 1,500 becquerels per litre and met international safety standards.
Japan has discharged approximately 163,800 cubic metres of ALPS-treated water in batches since the
in August 2023. The IAEA has confirmed that the tritium levels in the first 21 batches were also far below the operational limits set by Japan.

The water was accumulated after the NPP was crippled by the massive earthquake and tsunami that struck northeastern Japan in 2011 resulting in the core meltdown of three reactors. Water was used to cool the reactors. In total, 1.34m tonnes of radioactive wastewater is stored in about 1,000 tanks at the plant, which are almost full and need to be emptied to enable decommissioning of the plant to proceed.

The processed water is diluted with seawater to one-fortieth of the concentration permitted under Japanese safety standards before being released one kilometre off the power plant via an underwater tunnel.

title: CFS secures fusion funding boost
author: Tracey
text: Commonwealth Fusion Systems aims to deliver grid-scale fusion electricity in the early 2030s.Share
Conceptual rendering of the SPARC commercial fusion energy facility in Devens, Massachusetts (Credit: CFS)

US start-up Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) has raised $1bn of additional equity financing. This is the single largest funding round among fusion energy companies worldwide since CFS announced its $1.8bn Series B round in 2021. With this capital, and the $863m the company raised last year, CFS has now raised a total of $4bn – about 30% of the total capital raised by the fusion industry to-date.

CFS will use the funds raised to further accelerate its progress to commercialisation. In parallel with completing the assembly of its SPARC fusion demonstration machine, CFS is continuing to develop, what it intends to be the world’s
first grid-scale fusion power plant
, ARC, at the company’s Fall Line Fusion Power Station in Chesterfield County, Virginia.

SPARC does not stand for a rigid, word-for-word technical acronym, but is instead a play on words derived from its commercial successor, ARC. Specifically, SPARC represents the Soonest/Smallest Possible ARC – ARC stands for Affordable, Robust, Compact. ARC is the commercial, grid-scale 400 MWe power plant designed to deliver clean energy to utility companies.

SPARC is a pilot tokamak reactor that is currently roughly 75-80% structurally complete. The team is completing the installation of 18 large 20-tesla high-temperature superconducting magnets to achieve first plasma. CFS intends to utilise SPARC to cross the critical “scientific breakeven” threshold generating more energy from a fusion reaction than it takes to heat the plasma by 2027.
Having become the first fusion company to submit an application to PJM Interconnection, the largest wholesale electricity market in the US, CFS aims to
put power on the grid in the early 2030s

, bolstered by strategic partnerships with Dominion Energy as well as Google and Eni, two investors in CFS that also signed power purchase agreements (PPAs) to buy more than half the power the plant will produce.

“CFS is making what once was impossible into inevitable. In the 2030s, we will put commercial fusion on the grid,” said Bob Mumgaard, CFS CEO & Co-founder. “We have the science that works and the proven execution that’s consistently validated by the market. We regularly welcome investors from around the world to our headquarters in Devens, Massachusetts, where they see real and tangible progress as we ready support systems and finalise the assembly of SPARC. In unlocking commercial fusion energy, we’re on a path to make an impact at a civilisational level.”

title: Oyster Creek eyes SMR revival
author: Tracey
text: The former New Jersey nuclear plant is planned for transformation into a 1,360 MWe clean energy hub powered by four SMR-300 reactors.Share
Rendering of the proposed Oyster Creek Small Modular Reactor (SMR) project (Credit: Holtec International)

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (NRC) has approved the Licence Termination Plan (LTP) for Holtec International’s Oyster Creek Generating Station in Lacey Township, New Jersey. With the decommissioning and dismantlement of the site more than half complete, NRC approval establishes the official roadmap for the final radiological cleanup and release of the site.

“We believe the NRC’s approval is a testament to the quality of our technical work, the strength of our regulatory engagement, and our culture of safety and accountability throughout the decommissioning process,” said Oyster Creek Site Vice President Jeff Dostal. “The approved LTP provides the roadmap for the final phase of decommissioning and site restoration. We will continue to execute the remaining work with the same discipline, professionalism, and focus on safety that have guided the project to date.”
Oyster Creek began producing electricity in December of 1969. It was the oldest operating commercial nuclear power plant in the US until it
in September 2018, having produced more than 192 TWh of electricity over its lifetime.

Holtec International now plans to transform the retired Oyster Creek Generating Station into an advanced clean energy hub featuring small modular reactors (SMRs). The transition from a decommissioned asset to an active generation hub relies on a two-track redevelopment strategy. Holtec plans to construct four of its proprietary SMR-300 units at the site. The

is an advanced, passively safe, pressurised light water with a capacity of 300 MWe /1050 MWt and a design life of 80 years. It uses a single heat transfer circuit and houses a core of 69 Framatome GAIA fuel assemblies. Each assembly uses standard ceramic pellets containing up to 5% enriched uranium dioxide avoiding the need for specialised, hard-to-source fuels. The used fuel pool is located entirely inside the fortified containment structure.

The new configuration will deliver a combined 1,360 MWe – more than twice the 636 MWe capacity of the original plant, which ceased operations in 2018. Holtec has targeted 2036 for commercial operation of all four units. The project is classified in the “Development Phase,” conditional on state and local support, financing, and equity arrangements. The project was accelerated by
lifting in April of New Jersey’s 40-year nuclear moratorium

Because the site already has robust grid connections, Holtec is exploring the integration of AI data centres directly alongside the new nuclear facility to consume the baseload power. Redevelopment is expected to create 4,000 temporary construction jobs and over 400 permanent operational roles, boosting the local supply chain.
plans to deploy two SMR-300 units

(Pioneer-1 and Pioneer-2) at its Palisades NPP site in Michigan adjacent to the existing 800 MWe main plant. NRC has accepted Part 1 of Holtec’s phased construction permit application for review with Part 2 scheduled for submission by mid-2027. The NRC and the US Army Corps of Engineers are compiling a draft Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). NRC’s formal review schedule targets March 2027 for issuing the final safety evaluation and environmental impact reports. A decision regarding the Limited Work Authorisation (LWA) is slated for June 2027 after which nuclear island construction an begin.
In December 2025, the project
received a $400m matching grant

from the Department of Energy (DOE) specifically allocated to accelerate SMR-300 deployment. Holtec and its global construction partner, Hyundai Engineering & Construction, have completed early site clearing and geotechnical data collection. Following construction, Holtec intends to file an Operating Licence Application in 2028, with the units slated to begin commercial service in the early 2030s.

title: Aalo targets nuclear-powered AI
author: Tracey
text: The first proof-of-concept deployment is planned for 2027 at Idaho National Laboratory.Share

US AI factory company Crusoe and nuclear start-up Aalo Atomics have entered a strategic partnership focused on developing and deploying the first nuclear-powered AI Factory data centre designed to validate nuclear power’s effectiveness with AI workloads. The deal follows Aalo’s Aalo-X test reactor
achieving nuclear criticality
on 4 July 2026 under the Department of Energy’s (DOE’s)

In 2027 Aalo plans to initially power a Crusoe Spark modular data centre, running Crusoe Cloud, at Idaho National Laboratory (INL) as a proof of concept. Crusoe Spark is a turnkey, prefabricated modular AI data centre unit designed to function as a self-contained “AI factory”. It is a highly portable, outdoor-rated chassis slightly larger than a standard physical shipping container: Each individual container draws roughly 1 MWe of power.
The Aalo-X is an experimental, extra-modular reactor (XMR) that uses sodium as a coolant and is fuelled by low-enriched uranium dioxide. The test reactor is the precursor to the

, a 50 MWe XMR power plant purpose-built for data centres. Each fully modular Aalo Pod will contain five factory-built, sodium-cooled, Aalo-1 reactors, using low-enriched uranium dioxide fuel. Looking forward, Aalo and Crusoe intend to deploy Aalo Pods and Aalo’s 50 MWe XMR power plants at Crusoe data centres, by the end of 2029.

“The next generation of AI infrastructure demands power that is reliable, abundant, clean and at scale, and Aalo’s nuclear reactors are built to meet that need,” said Cully Cavness, Co-Founder, President and Chief Strategy Officer at Crusoe. “One of Crusoe’s core values is to ‘bend the arc of energy toward sustainability,’ and within that value we embrace the principle of using Crusoe’s market position to support and accelerate energy innovation. In line with our core values, we look forward to Aalo and Crusoe jointly demonstrating to the industry the first AI data centre powered by a small modular nuclear reactor.”
Matt Loszak, Aalo Atomics CEO, noted: “As one of only four companies to reach criticality by President Trump’s deadline for companies in the DOE

, we are now well positioned for not only the full power operation of our 10 MWe Aalo-X reactor, but also the deployment of the Aalo Pod to power commercial data centres. We are now the only nuclear technology company to design and build a nuclear reactor fuelled to produce 10MW of electricity– an achievement that positions Aalo as the premier power provider for the modern data centre.”

Aalo has already begun work on its second nuclear reactor (located next to the Aalo-X test reactor at INL), testing a commercial-scale system that will produce electricity and power for an on-site Crusoe Spark modular data centre.

title: Doicești SMR debate intensifies
author: Tracey
text: The Doicești SMR project is a flagship initiative intended to position Romania as the first country in the European Union to deploy next-generation nuclear technology. Share
(Image credit: Nuscale Power)

Romanian nuclear utility Nuclearelectrica has rejected all findings of illegality relating to its small modular reactor (SMR) project in Doicești, following a critical report by the Prime Minister’s Control Body (CCPM – Corpului de Control al Prim-Ministrului). In a formal statement to the Bucharest Stock Exchange, management stated that all decisions complied with the law, received full shareholder approval, and resulted in no quantifiable damage to the company.

The CCPM alleged significant irregularities in the Doicești SMR project, including 20-month delays, $3.8bn cost increases, and inflated land acquisition costs. Nuclearelectrica countered that these findings constitute commercial opinions rather than legal infractions, stating the project complied with regulations and that site selection was validated by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

The Doicești SMR project is a flagship initiative intended to position Romania as the first country in the European Union to deploy next-generation nuclear technology. The project will replace a former 600 MWe coal-fired thermal plant in Doicești with a clean energy complex. It is managed by RoPower Nuclear, a 50/50 joint venture between state-owned Nuclearelectrica and private energy company Nova Power & Gas.

The facility is designed to use NuScale Power’s VOYGR-6 technology, aiming for a total capacity of 462 MWe using six 77 MWe reactor modules. To minimise risk and manage the estimated $6-7bn cost, Romania plans to build and test just one module first before committing to the remaining five. The initial memorandum of understanding (MOU) between Nuclearelectrica and US-based NuScale Power was signed in 2019 to evaluate SMR technology and firm plans for deployment were announced in 2021. The Doicești site was selected in May 2022 and the following September RoPower Nuclear was launched to oversee project engineering and development.

Front-End Engineering & Design (FEED 1 and FEED 2) technical phases were executed in 2023-24 alongside site evaluations backed by the IAEA. In February shareholders approved the Final Investment Decision (FID), transitioning the project from the analytical phase into active implementation. Technical deadlines required finishing the final groundwork in May, including geotechnical surveys, licensing continuation, and Pre-EPC (Engineering, Procurement, and Construction) organisation.

A 15-month Pre-EPC phase is now underway to finalise specific engineering costs, choose heavy-industry contractors, and secure definitive project financing. The targeted commercial operation date for the first 77 MWe pilot reactor module is 2033 with full operational capacity of all six SMR modules to follow in 2034, provided the initial testing unit meets commercial and safety expectations.

The 10-page CCPM report detailed serious irregularities concerning the Doicești SMR project, claiming that certain structural decisions effectively left state-owned Nuclearelectrica “outside the protection of corporate law”. Nuclearelectrica countered each point, filing an extensive 13-page defence to shareholders via the Bucharest Stock Exchange. Nova Power & Gas also rejected the findings of the CCPM report strongly disputing the allegations regarding the Doicești site transaction, calling the report’s conclusions inaccurate.
