The financial backing is structured around four primary mechanisms. Before major construction begins, Korea Eximbank completely funds early-stage technical and economic feasibility studies. This includes covering the ongoing dual-phase valuation of the BNPP rehabilitation potential SMR grids.

Barakah NPP in UAE, Korea Eximbank launched a specialised K-Finance Package. For the Philippines, this means providing customised sovereign loan structures with extended repayment grace periods to match the lengthy construction timelines of nuclear plants. It also includes offering low-interest project financing directly to Filipino utility consortia if they choose South Korean technology.

Through a landmark tripartite agreement signed with KHNP and Meralco in March, Korea Eximbank provides bilateral credit lines and loan guarantees. ensures that if a local utility signs a contract for a Korean reactor, Eximbank steps in to cover the high upfront capital expenditure (CapEx), drastically reducing the debt-to-equity pressure on the local utility’s balance sheet.

Korea Eximbank is not a new player in the Philippine market. The state lender holds deep institutional credibility in Manila, having previously acted as the primary project financier for major conventional energy milestones in the country, including the Ilijan and Cebu power plants. Local conglomerates view this existing relationship as a safety net against project delays or capital shortfalls.

title: Site handover advances Polish NPP
author: Tracey
text: Early construction works are scheduled to begin ahead of first concrete in 2028 and first unit operation in 2036.Share

The project to build Poland’s first NPP is progressing, with general contractor Bechtel taking over management of the 330-hectare site in Pomerania from the state-owned project company Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ). With this transition, Bechtel officially assumes full responsibility for site coordination and management.

By taking over the comprehensive coordination of direct activities at the future construction site. Bechtel will be responsible for both the execution and supervision of the work carried out at this stage, as well as cooperation with investment subcontractors, and for safety at the construction site, PEJ said. Tasks will be carried out by Bechtel employees, including from the company’s newly opened office in Pomerania. As the investment progresses, the importance of the Gdańsk branch will grow to become Bechtel’s main operational and engineering base as part of the AP1000 project.

In November 2022, the then Polish government selected Westinghouse AP1000 reactor technology for a three-unit NPP, to be built at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in the Choczewo municipality in Pomerania. An agreement setting a plan for the delivery of the plant was signed in May 2023 by Westinghouse, Bechtel and PEJ. In September 2023, an engineering development agreement (EDA) was signed with Westinghouse and Bechtel to finalise a site-specific design for the NPP.

The Ministry of Climate & Environment issued a decision-in-principle in July 2024 for PEJ to construct the plant. In December 2025, PEJ signed an amendment to the EDA to accelerate preparatory work. According to the draft update of the Polish Nuclear Energy Programme (PPEJ – Program Polskiej Energetyki Jądrowej) commercial operation of the first unit is expected to begin in 2036. First concrete is scheduled for late 2028.

Simultaneously with Bechtel’s takeover, domestic construction company Budimex SA secured a PLN208.88m $55.8m) contract to spearhead the initial earthworks phase. This contract marks the transition from purely administrative design phases to active physical deployment. The initial engineering scope assigned to Budimex focuses entirely on establishing infrastructure in preparation for construction.

Work will include levelling of the land; reconstruction and extension of drainage systems; and construction of a network of temporary roads with a total length of approximately 16 km. Over a 300-hectare area on the construction site, work will be carried out to level the ground. Additional embankments will be built to prepare the area for the start of basic construction work. Approximately 6 km of drainage ditches will be built, along with culverts and erosion protection.

In parallel, work will be carried out to prepare areas for future technical, logistical and production facilities and to adapt existing infrastructure. New infrastructure will also be built, including fuel storage and vehicle refuelling facilities, car washes, equipment maintenance workshops, storage yards and material storage facilities, as well as office, social and sanitary facilities. The work is scheduled to take place between the third quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2029.

“After years of preparation, research and obtaining the necessary administrative decisions, we are entering a phase of intensive field work,” said Marek Woszczyk, President of the PEJ Management Board. “This is clear evidence that the Polish nuclear programme is moving from plans to implementation. Already more than 200 people are working on the site, and in the coming months this number will systematically increase. Entrusting Bechtel with the coordination of work will allow us to maintain the assumed pace of implementation and effectively prepare the project for the next stages of construction.”

Leszek Hołda, President of Bechtel Polska, noted: “This is a very important day both for Bechtel and for the implementation of the entire, multi-year project of building an infrastructure and energy project that is crucial from the point of view of our country – the first NPP in Poland. We formally become the hosts of the construction site, taking over this role from PEJ. This means moving the investment to the next stage – a phase of operational activities, carried out both by Bechtel’s engineers and experts, as well as specialised and local, contractors. Today we have also reached another milestone – we have started cooperation with an experienced Polish company that will be responsible for the implementation of the earthworks. Budimex is the fifth Polish company with which we have signed an agreement this year.”

Artur Popko, President of the Budimex Management Board, said Budimex has been participating key Polish for many years. “For nearly 60 years, this is where we have been building roads, railways, energy facilities and critical infrastructure. These are investments that benefit millions of people every day. I am extremely pleased that Bechtel – the general contractor for Poland’s first nuclear power plant – has trusted Polish contractors and entrusts us with the implementation of the first works that pave the way for further stages of this key investment. We are proud that as a Polish company we can participate in a project that will be fundamental to the security and future of our country.”

PEJ said the contract with Budimex is another example of the growing participation of domestic companies in the project – five contracts with Polish contractors have already been signed in the last few months. Since 2020, the company has concluded agreements with approximately 475 domestic entities with a total value exceeding PLN1.2bn, including 77 companies from Pomerania for approximately PLN370m.

In February, Bechtel also began cooperation with the Pomeranian company Grupa Doraco, including the preparation of geological and geotechnical research facilities at the site. In May, it concluded a contract with the Polish company Unihouse for the construction of employee facilities for 1,000 employees on the site, and in parallel is conducting several dozen tender procedures related to the project, the total value of which is approximately PLN1.7bn.

The total cost for the NPP project is estimated at around $37bn with local spending accounting for a large component of the overall programme Poland passed legislation to provide PLN60.2bn in equity support, covering roughly 30% of costs. The European Commission has approved Poland’s state financing framework. More than €14bn ($16bn) of the total project budget is legally designated to flow directly to domestic firms. Partnering with companies like Budimex and
embeds Polish industry into the regional nuclear supply chains. Bechtel has opened an operations hub in Gdańsk to directly transition local industrial capacity into civil nuclear expertise.

“The construction of the first Polish nuclear power plant is entering the next stage of implementation”, said Energy Minister Miłosz Motyka. “This is an investment that strengthens Poland’s energy security and sovereignty, increases our independence from external conditions, and creates conditions for ensuring stable and predictable energy prices for households and entrepreneurs.… Hundreds of Polish companies are already involved in the construction of the power plant, providing the services, technologies and competences necessary to carry out this investment. Our goal is to ensure that as much of the value of this project as possible remains in the country – strengthening the potential of Polish businesses, creating high-quality jobs, developing national competencies and building lasting advantages for the Polish economy for decades to come.”

title: Holtec eyes Southern US SMR growth
author: Tracey
text: Holtec, along with Entergy and Hyundai E&C will explore SMR-300 deployment across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas to meet rising AI and industrial power demand.Share
(Photo credit: Holtec International)

Holtec International has formalised a non-binding memorandum of agreement (MOA) with Entergy Services and South Korea’s Hyundai Engineering & Construction (HDEC) to explore the deployment of SMR-300 small modular reactors (SMRs) across the American South to meet the soaring baseload demand of AI-driven data centres, heavy advanced manufacturing, and industrial plants. The MOA was signed by Entergy Executive Vice President & Chief Nuclear Officer John Dinelli, Holtec CEO Dr Kris Singh and Hyundai Engineering & Construction CEO Hanwoo Lee.

The target region is Entergy’s four-state utility footprint across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas. The aim is to evaluate consumer energy demand, identify viable geographic candidate sites, and define commercial configurations. If plans advance, the projects will be built using a jointly managed project office. Holtec will lead the primary nuclear design and manufacturing, while HDEC handles the balance-of-plant engineering, construction, and procurement.

is an advanced, passively safe, pressurised light water with a capacity of 300 MWe /1050 MWt and a design life of 80 years. It uses a single heat transfer circuit and houses a core of 69 Framatome GAIA fuel assemblies. Each assembly uses standard ceramic pellets containing up to 5% enriched uranium dioxide avoiding the need for specialised, hard-to-source fuels. The used fuel pool is located entirely inside the fortified containment structure.
Potential projects in Entergy’s service territory would draw upon Holtec’s
planned SMR-300 deployment

at the Palisades site in Michigan, where the Pioneer 1&2 units are expected to become the global reference plant for future SMR-300 deployments. The construction permit application is under review by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), with pre-construction work taking place at the site. The expected completion date for the NRC’s safety and environmental impact evaluations is mid-2027 with final construction and operational grid connection targeted for the early 2030s.

The platform brings together the core elements required to commercialise advanced nuclear at scale – proven reactor technology, domestic manufacturing, integrated EPC delivery, and an operating reference plant. Major SMR-300 components are expected to be manufactured at Holtec’s Advanced Manufacturing Division (AMD) and future replica manufacturing facilities supporting fleet deployment.

“This collaboration represents another important step in Holtec’s strategy to commercialise the SMR-300 through strategic utility partnerships and its integrated delivery platform with Hyundai E&C and provides Entergy an opportunity to evaluate advanced nuclear as part of its broader, long-term resource planning considerations,” Holtec said. “As electricity demand accelerates across the United States, the collaboration establishes a pathway for the parties to assess where advanced nuclear may be needed to support industrial growth, AI infrastructure, grid reliability, and long-term energy security.”
In addition to Palisades, other SMR-300 deployment projects are being pursued in the US, and globally in the UK and Hungary.

At the Green River Advanced Nuclear Project in Utah, part of Utah’s “Operation Gigawatt” clean energy initiative, Blue Castle Holdings and Fulcrum Point Holdings (an affiliate of Hi Tech Solutions) established a joint venture to build a commercial nuclear plant based on SMR-300 technology, featuring an air-cooled condenser design suited for water-challenged areas. The initial strategic cooperation agreement was signed between Hi Tech Solutions, Holtec, and the State of Utah in 2025. The joint venture officially launched in May to advance the Green River site through immediate licensing and site development phases.
In the UK, Holtec and France’s EDF Energy formed a joint venture to

for up to four SMR-300 units at the former coal-fired Cottam Power Station (Nottinghamshire) as the Second-of-a-Kind (SOAK) project. The reactors are slated to power a 1 GW data centre project on-site. In March, the SMR-300 design cleared Step 2 of the UK’s Generic Design Assessment (GDA) process and in June the joint project proposal and Heads of Terms were formally submitted to the UK Government. The on-site data centre is expected to come online by 2030 using initial grid infrastructure.2030s with the SMR units targeted to become fully operational in the 2030s.
In Hungary an international expansion effort exploring Central European deployment is underway. Holtec partnered with Hungary’s state-owned energy company MVM to
of integrating SMR-300 technology into the Hungarian power grid. A formal memorandum of understanding was signed in December 2025 to initiate site and grid assessment frameworks.

title: Kozloduy decommissioning advances
author: Tracey
text: A new 10-year licence will consolidate decommissioning activities and radioactive waste management under a single framework.Share
(Photo credit: Bulgarian Nuclear Regulatory Agency)

The Bulgarian Nuclear Regulatory Agency (AYaR – Agentsia za Yadreno Regulirane) has formally handed over a new 10-year decommissioning licence to the State Enterprise Radioactive Waste (DP RAO – Drzhavno Predpriyatne RadioAktivni Otpadtsi) for decommissioning work at Kozloduy NPP units 3&4.

The new licence brings together and replaces the previous individual licences for the two units. It defines the safety requirements during decommissioning and gives the right to DP RAO to carry out deactivation and dismantling of structures, systems and components, as well as management of materials and radioactive waste from decommissioning processes.
The activities will be carried out in full compliance with the updated decommissioning plan for units 3&4. To reach the end state defined in the
Spent Nuclear Fuel and Radioactive Waste Management Strategy

, as well as the goals set in the Decommissioning Plan, DP RAO should dismantle all technological equipment in the engine room, reactor compartment and the auxiliary housing, which will subsequently be deactivated and transported off the industrial site.
All buildings and adjacent territories will be deactivated until the specified criteria for exemption from regulation according to the requirements of the
Safe Use of Nuclear Energy Act

(ZBIYaE – Zakon za Bezopasno Izpolzvane na Yadrenata Energia) and its implementing regulations. DP RAO continues to manage the decommissioning infrastructure projects financed by the Kozloduy International Fund through the European Bank for Reconstruction & Development (EBRD).

in April of Bulgaria’s first national repository for low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste, located near the Kozloduy NPP site. The repository will house the waste generated from dismantling these older units. The repository was primarily funded by a grant of approximately €76m ($89m) from the Kozloduy International Decommissioning Support Fund (KIDSF) administered by the EBRD on behalf of the EC and other international contributors. The project also received national co-financing totalling approximately BGN34m ($20m) from the Bulgarian government.

The aim is to decommission units 1-4 by 2030, aiming for a “brown field end state”. In addition to the repository, this is supported by the construction of the Dry Spent Nuclear Fuel Storage Facility, which began operation in January 2016 and can store used fuel for more than 50 years. The Plasma Melting Facility, commissioned in 2018, reduces the volume of and treats radioactive waste.

Kozloduy units 1-4 were closed some 20 years ago as a strict condition for Bulgaria’s 2007 accession into the European Union, following safety classifications assigned by the European Commission (EC). However, these Soviet-designed VVER-440/V-230 pressurised water reactors, built with notable technical design modifications. Though officially classified by the EC as older, non-upgradable V-230 models, both reactors featured a heavily modernised, improved design that bridged the safety gap toward the much more advanced V-213 generation.

Bulgaria continues to maintain its energy grid through units 5&6 and is currently making moves to expand the Kozloduy site with two advanced Westinghouse AP1000 reactors, projected to come online in the mid-2030s. There are also various proposals for the construction of small modular reactors.

title: AWS scraps Calvert Cliffs data centre
author: Tracey
text: Amazon has cited development and regulatory hurdles in cancelling plans for a 500 MWe data centre campus beside Maryland’s Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant.Share
(Photo credit: Constellation Energy)

Amazon Web Services (AWS) has officially withdrawn its application to build a massive data centre campus next to Constellation’s Calvert Cliffs NPP in Maryland. The Calvert County Government announced that Amazon Data Services had cancelled its Calvert Technology Center Conceptual Site Development Plan.

The conceptual site plan proposed eight data centre buildings spanning more than 2.46m square feet. The campus was projected to need around 500 MWe of power. The facilities were intended to be powered through a direct energy agreement with Constellation Energy, which operates the adjacent nuclear plant.

According to statements from AWS, the company chose not to move forward after evaluating development timelines, rigid operational requirements, and its ability to rapidly deliver capacity for customers. The decision also coincided with strict local regulatory hurdles. At the time of withdrawal, Calvert County was moving to vote on a six-month moratorium on new data centre developments to give local officials time to review zoning laws and heavy industrial use conditions.

AWS submitted its initial application in May paying both application fees and environmental health fees. As proposed, the Calvert Technology Center would have been Calvert County’s first large-scale data centre development, spanning three separate campuses on roughly 2,000 acres of Constellation Energy land adjacent to the Calvert Cliffs plant. AWS was planning to draw power through a purchase agreement with Constellation and connect to the regional PJM grid.

AWS representatives told Calvert County residents the project would not have required new water withdrawals, saying a data centre would tap into Calvert Cliffs’ existing Chesapeake Bay cooling water system rather than drawing additional water from the bay.

in 2025 with Microsoft involving the restart of a reactor at Pennsylvania’s former Three Mile Island site. The Microsoft agreement differs fundamentally from the cancelled AWS plan because Microsoft is buying power directly from the regional grid rather than building the data centre campus directly adjacent to the nuclear facility. The deal involves a 20-year power purchase agreement to buy 100% of the 835 MWe of electricity generated by the restarted Three Mile Island unit 1 reactor.

The project is on track to begin producing electricity by the middle of 2027, ahead of its original 2028 estimate. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approved a crucial waiver allowing Constellation to transfer grid capacity rights from its Eddystone natural gas plant to the Crane unit. Without that federal intervention, regional transmission constraints would have delayed the plant’s full power delivery until 2031.

The Department of Energy finalised a $1bn loan to Constellation to partially finance the $1.6bn overhaul of the turbine, main power transformers, generator, and cooling systems. The project cleared environmental hurdles by securing approval from the Susquehanna River Basin Commission to pull up to 73 million gallons of water daily to support operations, although it still awaits final safety and licensing updates from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

title: X-energy secures HALEU for Xe-100
author: Tracey
text: X-energy has secured enrichment capacity from Centrus for LEU and HALEU, strengthening fuel supply for its expanding Xe-100 advanced reactor programme in the US and UK.Share
Centrus Energy’s American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio (Credit: Centrus Energy)

US-based X-energy and Centrus Energy Corp have signed a definitive agreement whereby Centrus will provide X-energy with enrichment services for low-enriched uranium (LEU) and high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU). The agreement is intended to de-risks X-energy’s Xe-100 project pipeline and to secure HALEU to support a portion of the initial fuel needs of X-energy’s planned 11.5 GWe commercial pipeline.

The Xe-100 is an 80 MWe helium-cooled HTGR that can be deployed in modular 4-unit or 12-unit configurations. The design simultaneously generates grid electricity and high-temperature heat/steam. This makes it ideal for heavy industrial decarbonisation. It uses X-energy’s TRISO-X Tri-structural Isotropic particle fuel pebbles.

The X-energy-Centrus partnership combines the capabilities of the first two US HALEU fuel facilities to be licensed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). HALEU enriched by Centrus at the American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio will be supplied to X-energy’s fuel subsidiary TRISO-X, for the fabrication of TRISO-X coated particle fuel at its fuel fabrication campus in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. In February, TRISO-X received a 40-year Special Nuclear Material Licence from NRC enabling TRISO-X to commercially manufacture fuel using HALEU under a single licence.

HALEU, enriched to approximately 15.5% uranium-235, is the primary feedstock for X-energy’s TRISO-X coated particle fuel, and enables the Xe-100 to operate more efficiently, achieve higher temperatures, extend operating cycles, and deliver greater performance than conventional reactors fueled with LEU (enriched to around 5% U-235). These characteristics enable designs like the Xe-100 to provide both electricity, and process heat for industrial applications.

X-energy has a potential commercial pipeline for the Xe-100 of more than 11 GWe based on projects in the US and UK. Because each individual Xe-100 unit generates 80 MWe of power, this pipeline represents a global deployment of around 144 advanced reactors. The agreements underpinning X-energy’s major commercial projects were signed between 2023 and 2025.

In March 2023, Dow and X-energy finalised a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) to deploy a four-unit reactor plant at an industrial facility in Seadrift, Texas. In October 2024, Amazon Web Services (AWS) anchored an approximate $500m Series C-1 financing round for X-energy and signed a formal partnership to fund and deploy over 5 GWe of SMR capacity to power its data centres. Centrica signed a JDA with X-energy in September 2025 to establish a UK-based development firm and pursue a 6 GWe fleet.

The agreement allows for prepayments from X-Energy to Centrus “under a phased approach to scale HALEU production to the advancement of X-energy’s commercial pipeline. X-energy previously secured the initial HALEU required to fuel its Xe-100 project with Dow through the Department of Energy’s HALEU Availability Program.

Prepayment arrangements and government funding have mitigated uncertainties with advanced reactor developers needing to know they will have the fuel for their projects, while the fuel companies want to be assured of future demand before investing in new facilities. Centrus says it has a $3bn “contingent LEU and HALEU backlog, of which $2.4bn is definitised”.

“X-energy is pleased to take the next step in our strategy to secure a portion of the HALEU our current and future customers will need to deploy advanced reactors at scale,” said X-energy CEO J Clay Sell. “Our approach is to build a resilient, long-term fuel supply strategy by partnering with enrichment providers that are investing in new HALEU production capacity. Through our agreement with Centrus, X energy has secured enrichment capacity that will support our customers’ initial fuel needs through the market’s transition to a robust commercial HALEU supply.”

Amir Vexler, President and CEO of Centrus, noted: “This is another significant agreement that validates Centrus as the go-to, de-risked supplier of HALEU to the global market. Agreements like these provide important non-dilutive, non-debt capital to support our build-out and serves to advance commercial LEU and HALEU capacity expansion.”

title: Tri-party deal targets recycled SMR fuel
author: Tracey
text: Curio, NuScale Power, and Framatome aim to build a unified domestic supply chain for next-generation small modular reactor (SMR) fuel by recycling existing used nuclear material. Share

A new strategic partnership brings together US-based Curio, NuScale Power Corporation, and Framatome Inc (the US-based regional subsidiary of France’s Framatome) to build a unified domestic supply chain for next-generation small modular reactor (SMR) fuel by recycling existing used nuclear material. The memorandum of understanding (MOU) addresses a critical challenge in the energy sector – establishing an integrated, closed-loop fuel cycle that reduces waste and secures energy independence.

The partnership divides tasks according to each company’s specialised expertise. Curio supplies the recycling mechanism, through its proprietary technology to dramatically clean up waste. It is designed to reduce residual nuclear waste volumes by up to 97% while reclaiming valuable, strategic nuclear materials. As a provider of advanced SMRs, NuScale provides the technical blueprints and exact fuel requirements needed for its advanced reactor designs. Framatome offers massive industrial scaling capabilities, including fuel fabrication, qualification, and established commercial supply logistics.
The three-way collaboration is structured around a few major milestones:
Pathways evaluation: mapping out “source-to-fuel” and “source-to-product” channels using materials recycled by Curio.
Commercialisation: syncing future engineering efforts to easily qualify and mass-fabricate advanced nuclear fuels.
Market integration: smoothing supply chain bottlenecks to easily move next-generation fuel streams from the processing plant into domestic and global commercial markets.

The agreement marks a progressive shift for the American nuclear energy landscape. Commercial nuclear fuel recycling had been restricted in the US since 1977, converting used fuel into static high-level waste. This joint effort aligns directly with recent federal initiatives, such as the US Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) CURIE programme, which funds modern reprocessing technologies to handle nuclear waste cleanly and build an entirely secure, domestic fuel market.

The Converting UNF Radioisotopes Into Energy (CURIE) programme, launched in March 2022, is a federal research initiative managed by the DOE’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E). It provides funding to develop advanced, commercially viable nuclear recycling technologies that process used nuclear fuel (UNF). The initiative funds projects designed to safely reprocess waste from light-water reactors by focusing on several core engineering developments, These include: waste reduction (separating actinide elements from nuclear waste to radically diminish high-level waste volumes); safeguards & monitoring (integrating real-time facility monitoring and ultra-precise material accountancy to prevent the proliferation of weapons-grade material); and cost efficiency (designing modular reprocessing facilities and performing techno-economic analyses to ensure recycled fuel can financially compete with freshly mined uranium).

In October 2022 the DOE announced its selectees, awarding $38m to 12 projects led by university labs, private developers, and national laboratories. Early projects entered their operational active phases in March 2023, including Curio’s NuCycle contract which received $5,000,000 in funding.

“America’s ability to lead the next era of nuclear energy will depend on more than building reactors – it will require building the fuel cycle infrastructure needed to support them,” said Curio CEO Ed McGinnis. “This collaboration brings together leaders in fuel recycling, fuel development, and advanced reactor deployment to evaluate innovative pathways that could strengthen domestic and international energy security, enhance fuel supply resilience, and unlock greater value from existing nuclear materials. By connecting these critical elements of the nuclear value chain, we are helping lay the foundation for a future of clean, sustainable energy.”

By evaluating opportunities across the entire value chain, the three companies aim to identify pathways that could support the commercialisation of advanced fuels and fuel-cycle solutions needed to power the next generation of nuclear energy systems.

“Advancing the next generation of nuclear energy demands bold innovation and strong alignment across the entire fuel cycle,” said Tony Robinson, Framatome Inc. President and CEO. “At Framatome, we are committed to working with partners who share that vision and support efforts to strengthen America’s nuclear infrastructure. This collaboration represents the kind of forward-looking, integrated approach needed to unlock new fuel technologies, and ensure the U.S. remains at the forefront of safe, reliable, carbon-free nuclear power.”

NuScale Power President & CEO John Hopkins noted: “With the most near-term deployable SMR technology, NuScale has long recognised that the nuclear industry requires a strong, reliable, sustainable frontend and backend fuel supply to meet increasing demand. We are pleased to work alongside our partners Curio and Framatome to leverage our complementary capabilities, including NuScale’s position as the only SMR to have received US Nuclear Regulatory Commission design approval, to help advance a more resilient and integrated nuclear fuel cycle for off-takers in the United States and internationally.”

Under the MOU, the companies will conduct technical assessments, feasibility studies, supply chain analyses, and interface evaluations to identify potential opportunities for future development agreements and commercial partnerships. They will evaluate how recovered materials from used nuclear fuel can support future fuel and product streams, while leveraging each organisation’s expertise across fuel recycling, fuel development, manufacturing, qualification, and advanced reactor deployment.

title: Criticality for Mochovce 4
author: Tracey
text: The 471 MWe VVER-440 unit will now undergo physical testing and progressive power increases before its planned first electricity delivery to the grid at the end of summer.Share
(Photo credit: Oenergetice)

Slovak power utility Slovenské elektrárne (SE) said unit 4 of the Mochovce NPP had achieved criticality before achieving its minimum controlled power level shortly after. SE said this demonstrates the reactor’s readiness for final testing phases before commercial electricity generation begins.

“Achieving criticality and minimum controlled power is the result of the work of thousands of experts who participated in the preparation, construction, inspection, and commissioning of the fourth unit. It confirms that the power plant is ready to proceed to the next testing phase before starting electricity production,” said Mochovce Project Director Martin Mráz.

This step will be followed by physical tests and tests at different increasing power levels to verify the behaviour of all power plant systems under operating conditions and prepare the unit for connection to the electricity system. The start-up process will subsequently culminate in a 144-hour demonstration run at full output. The timeline depends on the progress and results of the individual tests. Unit 4 is expected to deliver its first electricity to the grid at the end of the summer.

Nuclear Regulatory Authority (ÚJD SR – Úrad jadrového dozoru Slovenskej republiky) authorised SE to bring unit 4 into operation in May. As no objections were filed against the decision, it became legally effective on 24 June. Fuel loading began on 29 June and was completed on 3 July.

Mochovce NPP comprises four VVER-440 units. Units 1&2 began operation in 1998 and 1999 and unit 3 began commercial operation in October 2023. Units 3&4 with a design life of some 60 years, will supply some 26% of Slovakia’s total electricity consumption.

Construction of units 3&4 began in 1986 but was suspended in 1992 and resumed only after a lengthy hiatus in 2008. SE puts the value of the entire project at approximately €6.7bn ($7.7bn), up from an estimated €2.8bn in 2008. With the addition of Mochovce 4, Slovakia will have six power reactors in operation. Slovakia also has two VVER-440 units operating at the
. With all six units in operation, nuclear power should cover approximately 77.5 % of domestic electricity consumption.

The history of Mochovce 3&4 is a catalogue of project delays, political upheaval, and ballooning budgets. The 39-year timeline begins in 1987 when construction officially begins. In 1991 work stalled following the collapse of the USSR and funding shortages. Construction restarted in 2008 under majority shareholder Enel, with initial plans to finish by 2012-13. Multiple delays followed due to post-Fukushima safety retrofits, cramped spacing for modern thick cabling, and ownership restructuring.

SE is owned by a 66% majority stake through an intermediary vehicle called Slovak Power Holding (SPH). In 2016, Czech energy infrastructure group Energetický a průmyslový holding (EPH) bought a 50% stake in SPH from Enel in December 2024. EPH exercised its early call option to buy the remaining 50%. Following regulatory approval from the European Commission in March 2025, the deal officially closed two months later. Currently the state holds a 34% minority stake, with shareholder rights managed via the Ministry of Economy. EPH (via SPH) holds the 66% majority stake.

SE is planning new units at Jaslovské Bohunice. In January, Slovakia agreed to build a Westinghouse AP1000 reactor at the site. In April, preparatory Front-End Engineering and Design (FEED) studies were formally launched under the US State Department’s Project Phoenix framework. Unlike the existing units owned by SE, this multi-billion-euro project will be 100% state-owned.

Financial advisors (Rothschild & Co) were contracted in January. Heavy construction is slated to begin by 2032, aiming for an operational launch by 2038–2040. Slovakia is also aiming to turn Jaslovské Bohunice into a regional testing ground for fourth-generation modular reactors. In June 2025, the state nuclear decommissioning company (JAVYS) and France-based start-up newcleo established a joint venture based at Bohunice. They plan to eventually deploy up to four 200 MWe modular reactors at the site. Separately, SE signed a memorandum with Synthos Green Energy to evaluate the feasibility of deploying GE Vernova’s BWRX-300 SMRs at the complex.

The expansion runs parallel to the ongoing teardown of historic site facilities. The old A1 reactor (shut down in 1977 after an accident) and the two older V1 reactors (dismantled as a condition of Slovakia entering the European Union) are in the final phases of environmental remediation and fuel cleanup to free up physical space for the new reactors.

title: TAE, Black Moon eye He-3 fusion fuel
author: Tracey
text: The collaboration could provide a future helium-3 fuel supply pathway for TAE's fusion power plants.Share
“Norm”, TAE Technologies’ current-generation fusion machine (Credit: TAE Technologies)

US private fusion firm TAE Technologies has signed an agreement with US start-up Black Moon Energy Corporation (BMEC) to support the future commercialisation of fusion power through a prospective helium-3 (He-3) fuel supply option and commercial development collaboration. Under the agreement, BMEC will supply helium-3 fuel to TAE.

TAE Technologies is one of the world’s oldest, largest, and highest-funded private fusion energy companies. The company, founded in 1998 and headquartered in Foothill Ranch, California, spent its first decade operating in near-total stealth. Instead of traditional magnetic confinement such as tokamaks, TAE developed a non-traditional, ultra-clean fuel cycle using a unique linear reactor design.

The firm initially incorporated as Colliding Beam Fusion Reactor, before changing its name to Tri Alpha Energy. The name refers to the three alpha particles (helium nuclei) generated during a hydrogen-boron fusion reaction. It rebranded to TAE Technologies in 2017.

Most fusion companies use deuterium-tritium (D-T) fuel, which releases high-energy neutrons that degrade reactor walls and create radioactive waste. TAE instead uses proton-boron, which is non-radioactive, safe, and abundant, but requires much higher core temperatures of around 3bn degrees Celsius.

To hold this superheated plasma, TAE uses Field-Reversed Configuration (FRC) – a linear, cylinder-shaped accelerator rather than a donut-shaped tokamak. Two spinning smoke-ring-like structures of plasma are shot from opposite ends into a central chamber at supersonic speeds, fusing into a hollow, high-stability “football” shape held together by its own magnetic fields. TAE uses massive high-energy particle accelerators (atom guns) along the reactor walls to continuously inject neutral atoms, heating and stabilising the plasma matrix.

TAE validates its physics through sequentially larger, more powerful machines. In 2015, their C-2U machine proved that sustaining FRC plasma via neutral beams was possible. In 2017, they turned on C-2W (nicknamed Norman after their late founder). Norman repeatedly broke company records, keeping plasma stable at up to 75m degrees Celsius.

In 2025, TAE proved they could form, heat, and sustain FRC plasma directly and solely using neutral beam injection, completely removing massive, expensive “formation sections” from the reactor body. This design iteration (demonstrated in the newest operational platform, Norm) dramatically slashes capital costs and hardware complexity. TAE is currently advancing towards Copernicus, a machine designed to demonstrate net energy capability using conventional fuels. This clears the runway for Da Vinci, their planned first commercial utility-scale reactor.

While proton-boron remains TAE Technologies’ preferred, ultimate pathway due to its abundance and zero-neutron output, the company operates with a highly flexible, multi-fuel design. TAE is exploring deuterium-helium-3 or helium-3-helium-3 via its agreement with BMEC for several strategic, physics-based reasons.

While proton-boron requires an unprecedented core temperature of 3bn degrees Celsius, deuterium-helium-3 fusion reactions occur at a significantly lower threshold of 500-600m degrees Celsius. This lower thermal demand allows TAE to commercialise their upcoming Da Vinci reactor much sooner. It serves as a commercial proof-of-concept while they spend more decades perfecting the physics required for 3bn -degree proton-boron containment.

The biggest obstacle to proton-boron net-energy gain is “braking radiation” (Bremsstrahlung). Boron has five protons and five electrons. A high concentration of electrons in a superheated plasma bleeds away energy as intense x-rays before fusion can occur. Helium has only two electrons. This dramatically reduces x-ray radiation energy losses, making it far easier to achieve a net-positive energy output at earlier stages of machine development.

The primary reason TAE avoids traditional D-T fuel is that D-T releases 80% of its energy as destructive neutrons. These neutrons require heavy shielding and inefficient steam turbines to capture heat. Proton-boron and helium-3 fusion are aneutronic or near-aneutronic. They release energy in the form of positively charged ions (protons and alpha particles). TAE’s FRC reactor can capture these moving charges directly using electromagnetic coils, turning fusion energy straight into electricity with up to 90% efficiency.

The TAE-BMEC partnership directly addresses one of the most critical logistical hurdles in advanced nuclear fusion – securing a reliable, long-term fuel supply for non-traditional fusion reactors. TAE focuses on advanced aneutronic fusion, which produces fewer or no neutrons compared with traditional D-T methods. Low neutron emission significantly reduces structural radioactive waste, making the reactor safer and longer-lasting. Aneutronic reactions allow the direct conversion of energy into electricity, bypassing the need for inefficient steam turbines.
However, helium-3 is exceptionally rare on Earth, requiring alternative sourcing strategies or future extraterrestrial mining concepts. The strategic goals of the TAE-BMEC collaboration include:
Supply chain security – establishing an early pipeline for critical fuels before commercial-scale reactors go online.
Market readiness – aligning technological milestones with commercial fuel availability to accelerate time-to-market.
Regulatory pathways – jointly exploring safety standards and commercial development frameworks for advanced fuel handling.

“This agreement can facilitate our path to power by providing an alternative fuel supply option,” said TAE CEO Michl Binderbauer. “TAE has a high degree of flexibility to select from the most cost-competitive fuel cycle, whereas many other fusion machines are able to operate only on the deuterium-tritium cycle; this provides TAE’s technology with future flexibility, depending on how fuel markets change over the long-run.”

BMEC CEO David Warden noted: “Developing a future supply chain for fusion fuels is a critical component of bringing fusion power to market. By working with TAE, we are helping establish the commercial framework needed to support next-generation energy systems.”

BMEC aims to pioneer helium-3-fueled fusion to address global energy demand and climate concerns, while simultaneously supplying existing high-value industries like quantum computing and medical diagnostics. The company plans to de-risk this long-term commercial strategy by launching a robotic lunar mission within five years to map resources, test extraction technology, and secure supply chains. Learn more about BMEC’s initiatives at the Black Moon Energy Corporation website. Binderbauer said the agreement with TAE provides the company with “future flexibility, depending on how fuel markets change over the long-run”. If aerospace companies like Black Moon successfully establish lunar mining in the 2030s, helium-3 might become economically competitive before terrestrial proton-boron systems are fully mature.

title: Akkuyu 1 nears first power
author: Tracey
text: Türkiye expects the reactor to begin test electricity production by the end of 2026.Share
(Photo credit: Atomic Energy 2.0)
Power generation from unit 1 of the Akkuyu NPP under construction in in Türkiye is expected this year, Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar told

. “Work to start the first reactor continues at full speed. We aim to complete this and start test electricity production by the end of the year.” He added that some 2,000 tests were being conducted in preparation for the launch.

Rosatom reported that a trial vacuum build-up operation is underway at unit 1. This is a standard pre-commissioning test in power plants to ensure the turbine’s steam condenser is entirely airtight and capable of maintaining a deep vacuum before active steam is introduced. The operation confirmed the readiness of the main turbine installation systems for the next stage of commissioning work.

Because steam turbines rely on a massive pressure drop to spin efficiently, any air leaking into the system will destroy that pressure drop and drastically reduce the plant’s power output. During this six-hour operation, engineers performed a number of technical steps. All external vents, valves, and access manholes on the massive condenser shell were tightly shut. Large, specialised vacuum pumps or air ejectors were turned on to suck the atmospheric air completely out of the system.
The steam turbine hall of Unit 1 at the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant
(Credit: Atomic Energy 2.0)

The main turbine was kept slowly rotating via its barring gear (a turning motor) to ensure the rotor blades and internal seals behaved normally under vacuum conditions. Once the target negative pressure was reached, engineers monitored the system to see if the vacuum levels held steady, confirming zero air ingress (leaks) from the thousands of joint welds and gaskets.

This test cannot be done in isolation; it requires a range of secondary support systems to function properly. Achieving a successful vacuum test proved that all the following systems were fully functional and integrated:
The vacuum system – the dedicated pumps responsible for pulling the air out.
Turbine gland seals – steam-sealing mechanisms along the turbine shaft that prevent outside air from rushing in along the rotating parts.
lubrication & hydraulic jacking – systems that lift and oil the massive turbine rotors so they can spin smoothly on the barring gear.
Thermomechanical monitoring – the sensors tracking metal expansion and bearing temperatures as the internal pressure drops.
With the airtightness of the condenser verified, the station can confidently move to the next major phase – the gas tightness test of the generator and hot functional testing using steam.

“Commissioning – is a sequence of interconnected control operations, each of which opens the way for the next one,” said Sergei Butskikh, Director General of project company Akkuyu Nukleer. “A successful set of vacuum in the turbine condenser showed that the main systems of the turbine unit are operating in design mode and are ready to receive steam from steam generators. This is an important result that confirms the high degree of readiness of the turbine for upcoming launch operations.”

The plant will eventually host four Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors. The pouring of first concrete for unit 1 took place in April 2018, for unit 2 in June 2020, for unit 3 in March 2021, and for unit 4 in July 2022. Rosatom is constructing the reactors according to a build-own-operate model. Work continues at the facilities of all four units and auxiliary structures as well as a new town for plant operators.

title: ZNPP staff injured by mines
author: Tracey
text: The incident was followed by a brief loss of external power, while operators began raising water levels in the spent fuel pools of all six units to extend cooling time during any prolonged loss of off-site electricity.Share
(Image credit: ZNPP on Telegram)

Four employees of the Zaporizhia NPP (ZNPP) were injured on the way to work as a result of an explosion on 7 August that took place after unmanned aerial vehicles mined roads in Energodar, ZNPP reported on its

channel. The injured personnel included members of the fire safety department, the departmental security service, and the transport workshop. Two of them are in a serious condition, and two others sustained minor injuries.

“The use of drones to lay mines on roads means that ordinary routes used daily by station workers, emergency services, and city residents become a zone of deadly danger. Any civilian vehicle, motorcycle, or bicycle could become a victim of such an attack,” ZNPP said. “Despite the ongoing threats, the staff at ZNPP continue to carry out their duties, ensuring that all safety parameters of the plant are monitored.”

The following day, ZNPP reported that external power supply to the plant had again been cut but was restored in less than an hour. “A short‑term interruption of external power supply occurred. The plant’s automation system activated and ensured a normal transition to a backup power supply scheme. The backup diesel generators started up automatically and fully supplied the systems necessary for the safe operation of the plant with electricity.”

ZNPP still depends on only the 330 kV Ferosplavnaya-1 line for its external power. The latest update by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi on 6 August said the recent rise in off-site power losses at ZNPP “highlights the fragility of the electrical grid serving the site and the need for continued efforts to help prevent a nuclear accident during the military conflict”.

He noted that ZNPP has lost access to external power twice in the previous week, bringing the total number of such events since the conflict began to 24, with 12 occurring in the past four months alone. “This trend, with the rising number of off-site power cuts at the ZNPP, is deeply concerning and clearly not sustainable,” said. “The Agency will continue its work to help improve the situation and support nuclear safety and security at the site.”

ZNPP has been without its main external power line, the 750 kV Dneprovskaya line, since March this year. The line was initially unavailable because of damage caused by military activity and was repaired in early June under an IAEA-brokered ceasefire. However, it remains unavailable because the substation that provides power to the line was heavily damaged by military strikes in May.

In another development, the IAEA team at the ZNPP was informed that the site has decided to raise the water levels in the used fuel pools of all six reactor units. The measure is intended to increase the time available before water could begin to boil off in the event of a prolonged loss of off-site power during which the site exhausted its diesel fuel supplies and could no longer continue cooling the pools.

The decision was taken in light of the prolonged unavailability of the 750 kV Dneprovskaya line and current challenges in resupplying the site’s diesel fuel stores because of military activity in the area. The work began this week, with the IAEA team present to observe.

title: Sogin takes military waste role
author: Tracey
text: Italy’s Senate approved legislation expanding Sogin’s mandate to include military radioactive waste to consolidate nuclear waste management ahead of construction of the country's planned national repository.Share
Sogin’s CEO, Gian Luca Artizzu (Credit: Sogin)
With the final approval by Italy’s Senate Assembly of bill No 2001,

decommissioning and waste management company, Societa Gestione Impianti Nucleari (Sogin) assumes responsibility for the treatment, conditioning and final disposal of all radioactive waste originating from the military research sector.

Sogin is now officially responsible for managing both civilian and military nuclear decommissioning and radioactive waste in Italy. The passage of Bill No 2001 closed a historical gap by legally expanding Sogin’s role beyond commercial nuclear power plants to include legacy defence research facilities.
Sogin continues its primary mission of decommissioning Italy’s four legacy NPPs (
, Garigliano, Latina, and Trino), alongside four fuel cycle research facilities (Fiascherino, Casaccia, Rotondella, and Saluggia), and the

. It now also takes charge of treating, conditioning, and disposing of radioactive waste from defence sectors. This includes the Navy’s RTS-1 Galileo Galilei reactor at the Joint Centre of Studies for Military Application (CISAM – Centro Interforze Studi Applicazioni Militari) in Pisa and the Euracos (Enriched URAnium COnverter Source) subcritical converter at the University of Pavia.

The final approval of the measure therefore represents a significant demonstration of confidence, initially on the part of the Government and now also of Parliament, in Sogin’s ability to manage highly complex nuclear interventions, for the benefit of the country’s security and in compliance with Italy’s international commitments.

“We are particularly pleased with Parliament’s vote because it confirms the trust already expressed by the Government towards our Society and further strengthens it, further expanding the scope of the activities entrusted to us in the nuclear sector,” said Gian Luca Artizzu, CEO of Sogin. “The inclusion of the activities relating to the Euracos converter of the University of Pavia constitutes an important recognition of the skills developed by Sogin and allows for the resolution of an issue that, within the scope of the obligations arising from the Non-Proliferation Treaty signed by Italy, had been at a standstill since 2012.”

The Euracos converter contains special fissile nuclear materials (highly enriched uranium or plutonium). Under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), nations must strictly control or eliminate weapons-grade material to prevent nuclear proliferation. To meet these obligations, the fissile core must be repatriated (returned) to its country of origin—in this case, the United States. However, the legal and bureaucratic process to safely extract and return this specific material had been completely stalled for over a decade due to regulatory gaps.

Sogin had worked with the US Department of Energy (DOE) and Consolidated Nuclear Security (CNS) between 2017 and 2018 to analyse and classify the Euracos materials, but without the official legislative power granted by Bill No 2001, Sogin lacked the mandate to take physical custody and finalise the operation. It can now use its advanced technical solutions, developed in tandem with the US government, to safely extract, package, and repatriate the fissile material to the US, permanently clearing Italy of a lingering non-proliferation liability.

As a result of the new legislation, Italy has eliminated fragmented management by placing all high-consequence radioactive materials under one state-owned entity. Centralisation ensures that both civilian and military waste are packaged to identical technical standards. This streamlines their eventual transfer to Italy’s future unified National Repository.

According to the National Inspectorate for Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection (ISIN – Ispettorato nazionale per la sicurezza nucleare e la radioprotezione), civilian Nuclear Waste comprises approximately 32,000 cubic metres. This includes legacy waste and structural decommissioning materials from Italy’s four shut-down NPP, medical facilities, and civilian research labs.

Military nuclear waste comprises approximately 894 cubic metres. This represents the total historical inventory currently stored at the CISAM military research centre, which includes very low, low, and medium-level activity. While military waste is tiny by volume, the structural core of the RTS-1 Galilei reactor holds higher concentration levels (medium-activity) compared to broad bulk demolition waste (very low-activity) generated at civilian sites. This is why Sogin’s specialised conditioning expertise was legally required to prepare these materials for safe storage.
The current official schedule for construction of Italy’s unified
National Repository and Technology Park

targets 2039 for the full operational launch. Sogin expects the final, single comprehensive decree approving both the chosen geographic site and the complete construction permit to be formally issued in 2029.

Once authorised, Sogin will begin building the surface repository, which consists of 90 reinforced concrete cells. The site will open for operations in 2039 to start receiving waste from around the country. The repository will intake the 98,000 cubic metres of legacy and future waste over four decades. By 2041, highly active residues resulting from Italian nuclear fuel previously sent abroad for reprocessing must be brought back and transferred into the facility’s temporary high-level storage complex. As the cells are filled, they will be covered by an artificial hill made of inert, waterproof layers. The site will enter a highly monitored, institutional post-closure control phase lasting 300 years.
In the meantime, Sogin is expanding local interim storage to secure waste at the source. For instance, Sogin
completed major civil works
on Storage Repository No 2 at the Enrico Fermi plant (Trino) in January. This newly modernised facility will hold ongoing decommissioning waste safely until it can be shipped out to the repository.

title: Changjiang 3 connects to grid
author: Tracey
text: The Hualong One reactor is expected to generate 18 TWh annually once fully operational.Share
(Photo credit: CNNC on Instagram)

Unit 3 of China’s Changjiang NPP in Hainan Province, constructed by CNNC Fifth Construction Company, has been connected to the grid and entered the load-carrying trial operation phase, China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) reported. Changjiang 3&4 are the first “Hualong One” project in the Hainan Free Trade Port. Unit 3, is expected to generate 18 TWh of electricity annually upon full operation, reducing standard coal consumption by 6.326 million tonnes each year.

Changjiang Phase II (units 3&4) involved estimated investment of CNY40bn ($6.4bn), according to China Huaneng, which holds a 51% share in the project. China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) holds the remaining 49%. The construction period is expected to be 60 months. Both units should be fully operational in early 2027.
The site is already home to two operating CNP-600 PWRs – Changjiang 1&2 – which entered commercial operation in 2015 and 2016. In 2021, CNNC also
of a demonstration ACP100 small modular reactor (Linglong One) at the site.

title: Bushehr workforce set for expansion
author: Tracey
text: The Bushehr NPP is Iran's first commercial nuclear reactor and the first civilian NPP built in the Middle East. Share
Satellite image of the Bushehr site in Iran (Credit: Atomic Energy 2.0)

Rosatom has said it intends to send several dozen more employees to Iran’s Bushehr NPP within two weeks, building its total project staff up to 100 by autumn 2026. This expansion is strictly conditional on there being no further escalation of the conflict between the US and Iran.
On 28 February, the joint military offensive by the US and Israel against Iran prompted severe security risks for foreign workers. Rosatom progressively

throughout March and April due to the threat of airstrikes near the 1,000 MWe unit 1 reactor, which continued to operate. By mid-April Rosatom had evacuated almost all personnel. It left behind a skeleton crew of 20 managers and safety operators to handle basic equipment integrity.

Moscow warned that military strikes targeting the immediate vicinity of the plant risked triggering a radioactive catastrophe comparable to the 1986 Chornobyl disaster. Following a brief ceasefire in April and a subsequent collapse of a peace framework in July, the situation has stabilised enough for a phased return of technical personnel.

Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev confirmed that construction continues on the site’s auxiliary buildings for power units 2&3. If stability holds over the coming weeks, the company expects to reach its 100-person operating threshold by the autumn.

quoted Likhachev as saying: “We have begun repatriating specialists to the construction site…. The first five engineers and technicians have arrived at their accommodation and begun their work – this brings the total number of Russian specialists to 25.”

The Bushehr NPP is Iran’s first commercial nuclear reactor and the first civilian NPP built in the Middle East. Its development spans five decades, transitioning from a West German industrial project into a major symbol of Russian-Iranian geopolitical and technological cooperation.

In 1974, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi launched an ambitious energy initiative aiming to generate 23,000 MWe of nuclear power within 20 years. In 1975, Iran signed a multi-billion-dollar agreement with Kraftwerk Union (a subsidiary of West Germany’s Siemens) to build two 1,200 MWe pressurised water reactors. Construction on unit 1 was almost complee before the 1979 Iranian Revolution.

The new Islamic regime halted the project, and Kraftwerk Union completely withdrew from Iran. During the eight-year Iran-Iraq War (1980–1988), the reactor structures at Bushehr were heavily damaged by repeated Iraqi bombing. Following the war, Iran attempted to re-engage Siemens to finish the project but Siemens refused in face of intense diplomatic pressure and trade sanctions imposed by the US.

In 1995, Tehran and Moscow signed an agreement for Russia’s state-owned entity Atomstroyexport (part of Rosatom) to complete unit 1. The project became entirely unique because Russian engineers had to perform the highly complex task of retrofitting their own VVER-1000 light-water reactor technology into the existing, war-damaged German infrastructure.

Commercial startup was delayed for nearly 15 years by technical incompatibility, funding disputes, and global pressure over Iran’s broader uranium enrichment programmes. However, Russia began supplying safeguarded fuel in late 2007 and unit 1 was connected to the grid in 2011 and full operational control was transferred to Iran in 2013.

In 2014, Russia and Iran signed a contract to construct two additional units (2&3) – Phase 2 – at the same site. Preliminary site construction began in March 2017, but construction has faced direct impacts from the ongoing geopolitical conflicts and funding difficulties.

Phase 2 represents a $10bn investment designed to add 2,100 MWe of capacity to Iran’s national grid. The primary financial and payment disputes that delayed Phase 2 stemmed from a critical €500m ($577m) debt backlog accumulated by Iran, exacerbated by heavy Western banking sanctions. These interlocking financial disruptions severely slowed down construction by restricting Rosatom’s ability to finance supply chains and pay contractors.

US and international financial sanctions blocked Iran from using standard global banking networks to transfer funds to Russia. In September 2021, AEOI Chief Mohammad Eslami flew to Moscow to negotiate an emergency instalment plan with Rosatom to clear the debt gradually. In May 2023, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak visited Tehran and formally confirmed that the debt issues had been largely resolved and reduced through specialised alternate financing mechanisms. Despite all these difficulties, Rosatom continues to classify Phase 2 as a top-priority project.

Unit 2 is structurally much further along than unit 3, featuring an upgraded AES-92 Generation III+ design using a VVER-1000/V-392 reactor system. Construction began in March 2017 and first concrete pouring was poured in November 2019. The reactor’s core catcher was installed in 2024. In January 2026, domestic engineering teams completed installation of the third ring of the internal containment building, raising the structure’s height to 40 metres. The fourth containment ring is scheduled for installation later this year.

Despite the temporary stoppage due to airstrikes in March, site work has resume with some 2,200 Iranian contractors working on reinforcement and concrete casting for the primary reactor building. Iran has revised the target operational date for unit 2 to 2029 due to the delays.

Unit 3 is in the preliminary phases of structural engineering. Initial heavy excavation and site preparation works began in January 2021. In September 2025, Rosatom and the Atomic Energy Organisation of Iran (AEOI) signed an updated memorandum to solidify cooperative logistics. Site activity is currently centred around secondary structural components. Likhachev confirmed that workers are building the auxiliary buildings and finalising preparatory infrastructure.

Metallurgical factories in Russia are currently forging the heavy blanks and cast metal components for unit 3’s primary reactor loop. Rosatom plans to begin shipping this core equipment directly to Iran by next year. Unit 3’s timeline is tied to progress at unit 2 and has been pushed into the early 2030s.

The Bushehr plant’s associated nuclear-powered desalination facility, managed by the Atomic Energy Organisation of Iran (AEOI), is a designed to turn Persian Gulf seawater into drinking water using the thermal energy and electricity generated by the reactors. Phase 1 (unit 1) infrastructure, a baseline desalination facility occupying nine hectares within the main power plant perimeter, was originally established in late 2022. It is designed to pull 2.5-3.5 cubic metres of water per second from the Persian Gulf.

In November 2025, AEOI head Mohammad Eslami announced an expansion programme to launch the fully integrated nuclear-powered framework. This upgraded system was scheduled to come online by the end of the current Iranian calendar year (March 2026), but the ongoing conflict stalled progress.

However, Likhachev confirmed that engineers are now preparing the hydraulic facilities required to safely feed seawater to the plant, effectively restarting the delayed timeline with the goal of bringing the 70,000-cubic-metre system online in the near future.

title: ORNL boosts Cf-252 production
author: Tracey
text: A new single-cycle chemical separation process will cut processing time by around 50%, helping ORNL respond to expected demand from advanced reactors and other industrial applications.Share

The US Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) is planning to increase production of Californium-252 (Cf-252), which is used to start up nuclear reactors and assay fresh reactor fuel, as well as for oil well logging, national security and other applications.

As the Western world’s sole producer of this rare radioactive isotope, the laboratory is implementing a breakthrough chemical process that cuts production time in half. A new single-cycle chemical separation process, which was nearly a decade in development, reduces processing time by roughly 50% without compromising material quality. Program Manager Samantha Schrell noted that a spike in demand is expected as advanced reactor designs move toward commercial deployment.

Cf-252 provides the initial spark of neutrons needed to ignite a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. A new nuclear reactor, or one that has been shut down for an extended period, has zero or very low background neutron activity. Without active neutrons colliding with the fuel rods, the reactor is completely dormant. Operators cannot safely start a reactor without a baseline level of neutron flux.

Cf-252 is used because of its unique property of spontaneous fission. Instead of needing to be struck by outside particles to split, it naturally decays and breaks apart on its own. As it splits, a tiny piece of Cf-252 fires out up to 100bn neutrons every second. For reactor start-up, the isotope is permanently sealed inside high-strength industrial capsules known as startup rods. These are physically inserted into the reactor core next to the fresh uranium oxide fuel rods.

Once the startup rods are in place, operators slowly pull out the reactor’s boron or cadmium control rods (which absorb neutrons). The steady stream of neutrons emitted by the Cf-252 begins colliding with the uranium atoms in the fuel. This causes the uranium to split, releasing more neutrons and triggering a controlled domino effect. Once the reactor achieves criticality and operates through its first fuel cycle, the uranium fuel, the fission products created inside the fuel will emit more than enough background neutrons on their own to sustain or restart the reactor. At this stage, the Cf-252 is no longer required to do the heavy lifting.

The surge in demand for Cf-252 is primarily driven by three types of advanced reactors, while the distribution process relies on a tight collaboration between the federal government and private industry. According to Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and industry reports, the commercialisation and legislative push for newer fission technologies require substantial amounts of Cf-252 as a reliable startup neutron source to initiate a predictable chain reaction.

Dozens of private companies are developing advanced small modular reactors (SMRs). Every newly deployed SMR core requires its own Cf-252 startup source. At the same time, US federal policy has shifted toward expanding high-capacity, domestic clean energy, aiming to kickstart the construction of 10 new large reactors by 2030. IN addition, the US military is executing directives to deploy compact, micro-fission reactors at domestic Army bases. These mobile or small-scale reactors require rapid, highly predictable startups, depending heavily on Cf-252.

Because Cf-252 is an intensely powerful neutron emitter, it cannot be shipped or used in its raw form. The distribution pipeline involves significant co-ordination. ORNL’s Radiochemical Engineering Development Center (REDC) isolates the isotope into bulk forms such as californium oxide, palladium-californium alloy pellets, or specialised alloy wires. The raw material is transferred to an industrial consortium of commercial reencapsulators. These specialised companies manufacture and permanently seal the radioactive isotope into heavy-duty, shielded industrial capsules.

Once securely sealed, this consortium distributes the finished, safe-to-handle industrial radioactive sources to commercial customers worldwide for reactor startups, oil logging, and coal analysis. For non-commercial use, the REDC Californium Facility directly administers the Californium-252 Industrial Sales/Loan Program, lending out specialised neutron source capsules to academic universities, research organisations, and other US government agencies.

title: Taipingling 2 delivers first electricity
author: Tracey
text: The Hualong One reactor will undergo further performance testing before entering commercial operation, with annual generation expected to exceed 9 billion kWh.Share
The main control room at CGN’s Taipingling Nuclear Power Plant (Credit: CGN)

China’s Taipingling NPP project in Huizhou has delivered its first kilowatt-hour of electricity, China General Nuclear (CGN) reported. This means that the second unit of the first Hualong One nuclear power base in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area has taken a key step toward the goal of commercial operation.

“After on-site confirmation following the grid connection, the unit is in good operating condition, and all technical indicators meet design expectations,” CGN said. “The unit will subsequently undergo a series of tests as planned to further verify its performance, and it is expected to be officially commissioned for power generation in the second half of 2026.”

Once fully operational, unit 2 is expected to generate over nine billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, meeting the production and daily use power demand of nearly one million residents and further strengthening CGN’s capacity to supply clean energy to the Greater Bay Area, said Zhang Guoqiang, Chairman of CGN Huizhou Nuclear Power, the CGN subsidiary responsible for the project.

CGN broke ground at the Taipingling plant in December 2019. With a total investment of over CNY120bn ($17.7bn), the project will have six Hualong One nuclear power units with an installed capacity of 1,209 MWe each. Upon completion, the plant is expected to produce more than 55 TWh of electricity a year, cutting standard coal consumption by around 16.65m tonnes and reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 50.8m tonnes a year. Taipingling 1 was
put into commercial service
in April. Construction of unit 3 started in June 2025, with initial grid connection scheduled for the end of 2027. First concrete for the nuclear island of unit 4 was poured in May.

CGN said that, during the construction of Taipingling 2, a series of digitalisation and intelligent technologies were widely applied. The project successively promoted the application of intelligent equipment and systems such as smart construction site, digital handover, and exoskeleton robots. It also implemented the first digital transformation project for spare parts management within CGN, empowering the full business process of nuclear power with intelligent solutions.

In addition, the project continuously advanced process innovation and technology iteration, achieving new breakthroughs such as using mobile aerial work platforms for nuclear cleaning of the inner dome and polar crane, and optimising the pressurisation and depressurisation rates of containment tests. It also promoted modularisation and automatic welding processes, and for the first time in a Hualong One project, innovatively applied integrated hoisting technology for frustum modules and steel liner base plates, providing strong support for improving quality and efficiency in nuclear power engineering construction.

title: Morpheus reactor targets data centres
author: Tracey
text: A two-phase study will assess current load needs of about 30 MWe and potential expansion to 100 MWe as the infrastructure grows.Share
Conceptual rendering of the Morpheus microreactor (Credit: Nuclea Energy)

Ontario-based Nuclea Energy has signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Miami-headquartered New Mining Co, a provider of high-density digital infrastructure and computing hosting services, to evaluate the feasibility of deploying Nuclea’s Morpheus microreactor to serve New Mining’s behind-the-meter power needs.

The MOU establishes a collaborative framework under which the parties will assess co-locating advanced modular power units based on Nuclea’s proprietary technology at or adjacent to New Mining’s data centre facilities. The evaluation is structured in two phases aligned with New Mining’s electrical load profile: an initial phase focused on engineering scoping for New Mining’s current approximately 30 MWe of operational data centre load, followed by a scalability phase evaluating modular expansion toward a cumulative capacity of up to 100 MWe as New Mining’s infrastructure grows.

The non-binding MOU does not constitute a power purchase agreement, virtual power purchase agreement, energy offtake contract, or any commitment to supply power or otherwise. Nuclea will not act as the operator of any nuclear equipment. The ultimate generation and delivery of power, if the parties determine to proceed, would be handled by a qualified third-party utility or specialised nuclear operating company to be separately identified and contracted. Nuclea will provide technical advisory services, including engineering specifications for its modular reactor designs, architectural planning for behind-the-meter microgrid integration, and initial regulatory and zoning pre-application strategy.

New Mining will provide site, engineering and power-usage data, in both instances to support the feasibility evaluation. New Mining is a US-based Bitcoin mining infrastructure operator with eight years of operating history and approximately 65 MWe of total capacity across facilities in North Dakota and Minnesota.

Nuclea’s Morpheus microreactor design is a lead-cooled, graphite-moderated micro-modular reactor, which will be factory-built, transportable and scalable from approximately 3.5 MWe to 50 MWe. Nuclea is targeting applications across data centres, defence installations, remote industrial operations and off-grid communities.

The Morpheus microreactor is currently in the pre-revenue, pre-conceptual design stage with no commercial reactor assets currently constructed or operational. The company is preparing its initial Regulatory Engagement Plan to submit to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to establish a formal licensing path. It secured a non-binding memorandum of understanding in June to potentially site a future nuclear test reactor for active demonstration at the Utah San Rafael Energy Laboratory and is currently moving through an 18-month commercialisation and licensing roadmap. The 18-month timeline is designed to transition the company out of this conceptual phase by funding and executing R&D, regulatory engagement, and prototype preparation steps. The capital to execute this transition is being raised through its strategic business combination announced in July with Mangoceuticals to achieve a Nasdaq public listing.

“High-density computing infrastructure is precisely the kind of behind-the-meter application our technology is engineered for, and this collaboration enables us to evaluate that fit rigorously alongside a partner who understands large-scale, mission-critical power demand,” said Nuclea CEO Josef Freundorfer. “The phased approach outlined in this MOU [with New Mining] reflects how we like to work: start with a clear-eyed technical assessment of an operator’s actual load profile, and let the data determine whether our technology is the right fit before either side commits to anything further.”

New Mining CEO Denis Slabakov noted: “As our infrastructure continues to scale, exploring reliable, carbon-free, behind-the-meter power options is a natural next step for our operations. Bitcoin mining is an energy-intensive business, and access to stable, competitively priced power has always been central to how we compete. We look forward to working with the Nuclea team to evaluate whether their modular reactor technology can support that goal over the long term.”

title: New robot cuts weld inspection times
author: Tracey
text: The device can perform inspections around 30% faster than manual testing while eliminating the need for manual scanning in hard-to-reach areas.Share

At Russia’s Atommash plant (part of Rosatom’s Mechanical Engineering Division) in the Rostov region, a new robot for ultrasonic testing (USC) of the quality of welded joints had begun operation. The device scans using two different methods and accurately determines the type of defect and its coordinates. Because the sensors do not need to be moved manually, the robot is 30% faster than a person in ultrasonic testing of products of complex geometry such as nuclear reactors and steam generators.

Currently, the company operates two robotic complexes for non-destructive testing of key NPP equipment, which makes it possible to completely eliminate manual scanning in hard-to-reach places and saves on consumables for ultrasonic testing.
